I may not have a lot of hours logged, but I feel like I can recommend the game due to one simple mechanic.

In other games where you level up there are typically two different ways the game reacts to your new power. Either the game is forever static, and you gain nothing further until you move on. Or the game keeps pace with you always keeping you on your toes.
Witchfire does something fantastic which is allowing you to choose when to make the world stronger. There's always incentive to challenge tougher enemies of course. More gear, story progression, upgrades, what have you. But sometimes you wanna go back to the tutorial area and feel powerful. Or you scrapped by with pure luck on that last run and wanna make sure you have timings down before the game throws new stuff at you.

While FPS games are not normally my go to, roguelites are, and so I was intrigued when I heard about Witchfire. The idea of a first-person extraction shooter rogulite with souls-like elements was too intriguing to ignore, and I'm glad I didn't.

The first thing you'll notice about the game is the production value. Visually it is stark but beautiful, with careful attention to detail to the surrounding environments. The gameplay is smooth and responsive, and offers the player a variety of ways to combat enemies, with many different gun types, spells, and even melee. 

The roguelite elements are admittedly somewhat thin. The Arcanas you grab during a run are the most obvious nod to the roguelite genre, but they're hampered somewhat by RNG. For example, in one of my most recent runs I was offered two Arcana at once that would've made me stronger against frozen enemies, despite the fact that I had no way to freeze them. In addition, many of the Arcana are simple damage/stamina boosts, which don't greatly impact a run. Having said all that, while I do wish the game would lean into the roguelite elements more, it is a ton of fun on its own.

Right now I would give Witchfire a solid 8/10, with a lot of potential to be an all time great in the FPS/roguelite genres.

I like games like this. It respects player agency. The game is, by dev's definition "normal difficult", and I totally agree.

Combat Difficulty:
The moment-to-moment combat difficulty can vary due to multitude of factors, but it largely boils down to understanding your loadout's strength and weaknesses, being observant to the terrain, and coming up with a gameplan to solve the encounters. The difficulty doesn't come from artificial gameplay designs, like spongy enemies, health-gating with immune phases, or generic rock-paper-scissor type design (think of early implementation of champions in destiny) Instead, it comes down to smart decision-making and resource management (stamina, spell usage etc.), utilizing the terrain to gain the upper hand in combat. Think of each encounter as a puzzle to solve. To spice it up, encounters in each run is randomly generated, so some runs will be easier or harder due to where things spawn on the map. On top of that, you have rogue-lite feature in terms of arcane, where you get to choose a perk each time you complete an encounter. Most of the perks are cookie-cutter, but it does add to the overall combat experience, where no one run will feel exactly the same.

Progression Difficulty:
The game uses souls-like leveling system, where you collect witchfire each run, go back to the sanctuary and level up your character. And I personally really like how the devs implement this, because it really feels like dark souls. Your actual character (the preyer) is not that much stronger or weaker compared to the random low-tier mob you encounter ingame (early on anyways, until you overlevel like with any souls game). This means the early-to-mid game balancing is really tight. This however, also means that you don't get the instant power up boost from leveling up. I can see how someone would've interpreted this as grindy, or artificial difficulty and level-gating, but that's simply untrue. At baseline your character is fully functional, and you really only level up to hit certain gear/equipment requirement, like in dark souls. Sure you can keep grinding and leveling up past those points but that's not how the system is designed to be engaged with IMO.

Aside from that, the game has world tiers in terms of gnosis system. As you increase your gnosis level, you gain access to more powerful weapons, spells, new locations etc, while the evil witch puts up stronger defences against you. Currently this system mainly serves as the main objective for the player to progress through the game, think of Warframe's planetary junctions' objectives. It's fine. It serves its purpose to ease players into the game, while giving players the agency to decide when they want to increase their gnosis level. You can spend a lot of time at gnosis I for example, grinding out levels and stuff to make the game "easier" if that's what you prefer, the game allows you to do that, like dark souls. However I personally feel you should aim to level up your gnosis sooner as it really opens the game up.

And of course, there's weapons, spells, equipments to boost your performance or make a build. You mainly acquire these from interacting with the mirror, which allows you to research these items, and you gain research progress by running missions or spending coins to fasttrack. You can also improve the performance of these weapons and spells by completing equipment-specific objectives and unlocking perks on it. These are not random. The Angelus (for eg.) will always have the shield perk, as with the other equipments. They all do fun and unique things, and they all feel good to use and shoot. Hopefully the devs keep adding more up to official release.


Overall, the game is fun as of now. All the systems are well-implemented, and synergistic of each other, and the game feels "tight" as a result. There's not much "artificial difficulty" to be honest, lest you be inattentive, impatient, unwise, and expect every single piece of information to be spoon-fed to you (instead of discovering and learning on your own).

[h1] So-called "powerful witch" when her opposition is a masked, mute lunatic with a gun and the ability to make fireballs with his hand (the latter will die at least ten times but he'll win eventually) [/h1]

[b] Witchfire [/b] is a REALLY fucking good game on the surface, but lord, it becomes insane when you find out this game is being made by a pretty small team of people (less than 50 I think), and feels almost AAA-ish in terms of presentation while being nowhere as bloody expensive. 

[h2] Gameplay [/h2]
[i] IMPORTANT NOTE: Witchfire is still in Early Access, so not only is it missing content, many of its mechanics are subject to change and addition. The last update overhauled progression pretty hard, so keep that in mind as the game still seems a decent bit away from getting finished. [/i]

Theoretically you [i] could [/i] describe [b] Witchfire [/b] as "the Dark Souls of FPS games" or whatever, but I honestly feel that doesn't really do it justice. You play as a Preyer, a dripped out, gun wielding fella with the ability to make gestures with his left hand to cause magic like he's in fucking BioShock. Over the course of the game (which takes place in several explorable locations as well as a central hub), you amass an arsenal of guns, spells and items that provide passive boosts, although you cannot carry everything at once.

Let's get right to the point, Witchfire is a difficult game. It doesn't start off terrifically difficult, but the difficulty quickly ramps up, especially as dying causes you to drop various resources (although you have the opportunity to retrieve these if you return to that area). To survive these encounters, you have the aforementioned guns and spells, but you also have a series of movement abilities. Using these abilities, you will be able to avoid enemy attacks, and in this game, any form of damage taken is significant as you cannot take much damage.

There's also a pretty cool upgrade system. The titular Witchfire is a resource primarily used to improve your stats, with there being six I guess skills(?) that improve some of 18 stats, with the cost increasing per upgrade. You can also upgrade your weapons and spells, unlocking unique abilities that, when used well, can be highly beneficial. It's all about the playstyles, with you being able to go all in on one skill or try to make a balanced build, as well as finding the weapon and spell setups that work best for you. And 

[h2] Story [/h2]
Witchfire doesn't have some crazy narrative or anything; it has a quick intro that pretty much boils down to "go kill the witch k thx", with a lot of the worlds details being conveyed through collectable letters and environmental story telling. It's not the craziest fantasy world, but it's pretty cool.

[h2] Graphics [/h2]
[i] Played on a laptop with 8GB of RAM, a GTX 1060, an i7 idk the model and a HDD [/i]

Witchfire runs pretty well on low settings, quality upscaling and most post-processing (except film grain) enabled, and doesn't look too bad, with the larger, more distant areas looking really cool actually. Of course, performance isn't without hickups, but these aren't too bad. The game has crashed on me a few times, suddenly freezing and stopping all audio, forcing me to either wait out the inevitable CTD or end it with task manager, but these aren't that frequent, and luckily crashing doesn't count as a death so your resources don't go poof.

[h2] Verdict [/h2]

While I still need to play it a bit more, [b]Witchfire[/b], in my opinion, is shaping up to be a game I'll be glazing for a while, and I might even end up putting it up there among my favourite FPS games such as DOOM Eternal, although we'll have to see. What I'm saying is

[h3] WITCHFIRE IS REALLY GOOD AND IT'S NOT EVEN FINISHED [/h3]

[h3]A solid and atmospheric roguelike shooter.[/h3]


[b]The game is fun and quite challenging,[/b] but you also have some control over the pace at which it becomes harder. The atmosphere is fantastic — creepy ambient sounds and unsettling yet subtle music seep into every corner of the experience.

[b]Each expedition run feels very Souls-like,[/b] but with a roguelike twist. Different maps have their own objectives and bits of story, though the narrative mostly stays in the background.

[b]The real core of the game is the combat[/b] — and it’s excellent. Gunplay feels satisfying and well-polished. There’s a wide variety of weapons to choose from, all upgradeable, as are spells, fetishes, and other items.

[i]Overall, I highly recommend it. For an early access title, it’s impressively well-made: looks great, feels tense, and runs smoothly with only occasional frame drops. There’s a bit of missing content here and there, but if this is just the beginning, the full release should be [u]fantastic.[/u][/i]

Even without levelling up, each time you re-enter a map, it is randomly re-filled with secrets, loot, enemies, and even new things to experience, all paced really well. Relatively simple gameplay, but well done. And excellent aesthetics. I always appreciate some semi-victorian semi-medieval witchcraft-themed games. I have been playing Witchfire since its very first Early Access release on the Epic Games Store. That’s why my playtime on Steam might look modest at first glance — but believe me, I’ve spent dozens of hours with the game. And every one of them was worth it.

I am absolutely delighted with the progress the team has made over time. The developers are consistently adding new mechanics, fresh locations, and intriguing story elements. Each update feels meaningful rather than cosmetic, and it’s clear that the game is growing in scope, depth, and size.

Most importantly, though, Witchfire simply feels fantastic to play. The movement system is fluid and responsive, rewarding skill and precision, while the shooting mechanics strike a perfect balance between weight and immediacy. Every encounter feels dangerous yet fair, pushing you to improve without ever feeling cheap.

The atmosphere is another highlight. From the haunting landscapes to the eerie sound design, the world of Witchfire draws you in completely. It manages to capture both the intensity of a fast-paced shooter and the tension of a dark, hostile environment.

In short: Witchfire already offers one of the most satisfying gameplay loops in the genre, and it’s still evolving. If the developers continue on this path, the final release could easily stand as the best dark fantasy shooter in recent years.

Witchfire is a game that I think has a lot of fun mechanics...in small, SMALL doses.

The developer says they believe it's "Fairly priced" but it's more like a demo in it's current state. $40 is a lot to ask for what is essentially a handful of stages with no variance. It bills itself as an extraction roguelike. It has little to no features of either.

Weapons are pre-set, and upgradable, and the overall core mechanics are fine, but the roguelike elements rear their heads at the very start of the run and pretty much never again. The upgrades are limited in quantity and the effects they provide tend to be very similar or unimpressive.

One thing I WILL praise the game for is it's graphics, sound design, and atmosphere. But that only lasts so long for a game based on doing the same thing over and over. A vista may be beautiful, a cavern haunting...but only the first handful of times you see it. After that, it becomes just another PNG. Just another hole.  And once you've seen the handful of events on a stage, it's done. There's not enough content to draw me back. The leveling system is soulsborne to it's core, and that is both a blessing and a curse. Each level feels like a slog, each run, a promise of miniscule progress.

The best I can say is that you should get it....on sale. $30, maybe. $20, absolutely. Because as a one-time experience, Witchfire can be a lot of fun. As a Roguelike? As an "Extraction shooter"? It's "OK". That's it. Just "OK."

There was a chilling feeling washing over me in the first hours of [i]Witchfire[/i], and it wasn't due to the ghosts breathing down my back. It was a sinking feeling that I had done all of this before... but where?

Open world zones with activities marked on the map?
Small dungeons I could descend into for a timed activity?
Stats I could improve using resources?

It wasn't until I picked up and fired my first revolver that it hit me. [i]Witchfire[/i] is a single player [i]Destiny 2[/i]... and I love it. It's everything great about MMO-style looter shooters without anything to get in the way. The game valiantly charges through the mires of hostile, addictive game design trying to mess with your gray matter, with no microtransactions or in-game purchases to speak of. Instead, [i]Witchfire[/i] hearkens back to classic ARPGs like [i]Diablo II[/i] and [i]Grim Dawn[/i], focusing entirely on your growth through various hard-earned means. Every delve into the witches' territory leads to some interesting decisionmaking, especially once the higher Gnosis (read: world difficulty) tiers are unlocked and the game starts getting really  mean. 

The game feels incredible to play, with immaculate sound design and spectacular particle effects. Weapons are the highlight, with excellent foleywork and great punch to each one of them. Machine guns spew bullets down range, while shotguns rip the air apart with their blasts. When I compare this game's revolvers to [i]Destiny 2[/i], know that I am doing so in the highest praise, as the latter game has some of the best gunplay this medium has to offer. Enemies die to bullets yes, but also glittering electricity dancing between them, or roaring flames colouring the surroundings in a faded orange light. With a dev team at the helm that utterly nailed it's dark gothic steampunk aesthetic, you're left with a compelling power-fantasy toolbox that feels great to traipse around in.

Probably the coolest part of [i]Witchfire[/i] is how cryptic the entire experience feels. You're almost completely isolated, a lone warrior against impossible odds, staging hectic raids into cursed territory just to put pressure on the enigmatic Witch. It's an extraction shooter, but also an RPG. It's a looter shooter, but it also has some survival horror and resource management mechanics. It's a game about shooting a lot of red-tinted ghost guys in the face until they go away, and about waxing and wayning power like a rollercoaster from hell. One minute you're obliterating whole swarms of enemies, and the next you're traipsing around a new zone in fear from the onslaught that's about to befall you. 

This is a really compelling little title that I could see easily being worth the asking price, with a healthy amount of content and some really fantastic weapons. If it looks up your alley (or the ghost of [i]Destiny 2[/i] is slowly dragging your mouse cursor over to the purchase button), you should really give it a try.

Witchfire gets this, no lengthy cutscenes, no companions chattering in  your ear, no quest logs full of fetch quests disguised as meaningful choice, just pure  addictive gameplay. And it's a genre fusion that sounds mental on paper, it's a first person  shooter meets roguelite, meets single player extraction shooter, meets souls like boss combat with light RPG mechanics thrown in on top. And that shouldn't work, but it does and it works so well, because every system serves the core gameplay loop, you drop into a run, you fight  through the map, you collect witchfire, the games currency and face a choice, push deeper for better rewards or extract and spend what you've earned.

Here's what blows my mind though, Witchfire is still in early access, it costs 30 quid and was  made by just 12 people, and yet it runs better than most triple A games do at full launch. No shader compilation stutter, no texture pop in, no mysterious frame drops when you look at a tree, it just works, and sadly in 2025 that's considered a huge positive. 90% positive steam reviews across  10,000 players, that's the result of quality gameplay meeting technical performance.

But here's where they really show their commitment, so they've been delivering massive  content updates throughout the early access period, Ghost Galleon and the Wailing Tower  came out in 2024, Witch Mountain earlier this year and Webgrave just dropped in last month.  It was a complete technical overhaul with new weapons, new maps and systems, and each update  actually works on launch day, no emergency maintenance, no twitter apologies, just solid  quality updates that work. And meanwhile triple A studios are charging 70 quid for games that  need 6 months of patches to reach basic functionality, and here's the astronauts charging half that for an early access title that's more polished than any of them.
 
Purchase this awesome game and support the Epic team The Astronauts!!!

Witchfire is a singleplayer buildcrafting extraction shooter with synergystic abilities and roguelite elements. I disagree with the comparisons to the Dark Souls series outside of the visual similarities -- the game shares almost nothing with soulslikes other than the loss of currency upon death and (sort of) the leveling system. It's like Destiny meets Tarkov, but with some safety valves to ensure that you never get totally screwed over. This game has some really unique mechanics, namely the focus/dash-stun mechanic and the Itinerant Portal system which sees squads of enemies periodically dispatched to hunt you down across the map. The gunplay is extremely solid, hence the Destiny comparison, and the sound and visual design are also top-notch. 

My main issues lie in progression and certain difficulty mechanics that feel uninteresting or unfair:
- The game doesn't explain itself very well. This is all well and good for an RPG like Dark Souls, but for a buildcrafting shooter game I would like to have access to percentage values for pretty much everything. A lot of items and abilities in this game are pretty vague about what they actually do, and I think any mystique it adds to the world is overshadowed by how frustrating it can be to not understand how to get your stamina bar to regenerate.
- The game is punishing; this is good. What's not good is what it punishes you for, sometimes. If you get "cursed" too many times (5 to be exact) in a run, the game will spawn a sort of superboss that will often kill you. You get cursed by taking damage... and some other stuff that is never fully explained. There is a certain enemy that seems to just give you 3 stacks of curse when it sees you, but not always. Generally I think the curse mechanic needs some work.
- Visibility & enemy AI can be really annoying. Sniper-type enemies will sometimes hit you from behind "soft cover" like tree leaves, and since they're technically in front of you you won't get a warning arrow telling you you're about to be shot at. This is extremely frustrating when combined with the curse mechanic, as you'll sometimes take a stack of curse for essentially no reason to a Musketeer who you can't see through the forest. The Curse mechanic is intended to punish you for playing carelessly, but this visibility issue can make it essentially random, and that feels quite unfair. Again, the punishments for getting hit in this game can be really nasty, breaking your focus and removing your ability to stun enemies while also giving you curse stacks.

Overall, I think Witchfire is a fantastic game, and I can't wait to see its final form. I recommend buying it on sale or waiting for the full release, but either way it's one to keep your eye on.

Refreshing mechanics, one of the best FPS's I've played in quite a while.

The controls are good, exactly what you'd want from a shooter. The movement is above average, you can scale most walls so the mobility although limited horizontally gives you lots of verticle options. It's really hard to get cornered in this game but it can also be hard to out-run difficult encounters if you don't have a nearby verticle wall to scale (Some enemy types don't have the movement options to close in, I mean the very aggressive mobs.)
That being said the game still plays well without that safety net in place, there's alot of focus put on target priority and dispatching the targets VERY fast. You quickly get overwhelmed and because of how enemy hits stagger/drain stamina you can get combo'd and end up without enough movement options to escape these scenarios, so you need to be fast about everything you do. Once enemies get close you have a pretty limited dodge count to avoid attacks before the stamina is drained and god forbid you make one mistake and end up combo'd to death.
This is a positive overall, the game is challenging because the players movement tools are limited. Very tactical design. It slows down the pace of the game compared to the average modern shooter but again this refreshing for a FPS in 2025, I really like it. The fast part of the game is how quickly your expected to tap their heads and dodge fast-charging attacks in reaction(While managing a fairly low stamina count), not the movement itself. 

As far as builds go it's a trinket/elemental system so you pick a weapon and play into the according element type. The guns have built in playstyles that become unlocked as you use the weapon and unlock it's unique features. My favorite is a sniper rifle that has high damage but low ammo count, it's gimmick is 3 headshots in a row restores 2 ammo and consecutive headshots increase crit damage. It's whole game is headshotting and dealing insane damage. 
I run fire spells to increase weapon damage to further play into heavy hitting aspect of this sniper and prioritize perks that do things like "Randomly double damage against burning targets" and similar deals. 
Just an example of how you build for damage in this game. Fairly simple definitely not the highlight of the gameplay loop. Weapons purely modify how you play the game.

You get a heavy spell slot, light spell slot, primary/secondary weapons, and an ultimate weapon which does exactly what you think. There's also rosary bead slots which you can hold multiple of and they just give you little buffs to play into the strengths of the weapon/build you've selected. 

So build are simple but they serve their purpose acting as a gameplay modifier, forcing a player to approach encounters differently, so this is fine. What is a little more unique is how the game actually plays. It's like an extraction shooter in the sense that you go in, loot, and get out. But within each level there are missions/dungeons/encounters that become accessible as you progress through the game via the Gnosis system. It's almost metroidvania in this sense only in that you return to earlier already explored stages to access what you previously couldn't. The Gnosis also makes this more interesting by increasing the difficulty tier/mechanics of the game even in areas you've already been each time you increase it. So basically you grow stronger and learn to play, and the game grows stronger and gives you more to learn in turn. For the difficulty level this is a nice accessible approach, but don't screw yourself over accidentally by rushing Gnosis upgrades before your stat tree. You can definitely scale the game beyond your capabilities if you're too good at clearing bosses/dungeons on your first try. It will let you make it harder before it's a good idea in short. 

Best way to describe this is refreshing. I played it a couple years back in early access and said it was probably my favorite FPS of the year, I stand by that now. This is definitely the most refreshing FPS I've played in quite some time.

A final note because some people seem to be misleading a bit: Farming. You do not have to farm in this game to progress BUT like dark souls if you die in run then die again without reaching your body you lose all your "souls" which are used to level.
If you die lots you'll find you need to farm, just like in DarkSouls. It's frustrating in the same way, I get that but its nothing new and it doesn't translate to needing to farm. It translates to putting more emphasis on not dying mid-run. This game rewards patient positioning and quick aiming. The positioning is key for a newer player don't just run in take it slow. (Maybe also don't run a low range build if you're new. Without upgrading the Arsenal stat weapons have REALLY short effective ranges in this game.)

Witchfire is a fantastic game, I've followed it for years and although I enjoyed the early versions as well, it has only improved over time. You can really tell how much care and passion the team has put into this project, and it stands out even more among the uninspired, low-effort games that become more common every year. Each time I come back to Witchfire there are new mechanics and improvements, and I'm reminded again what games can be when the developers behind them put in serious effort.

Witchfires environments are handcrafted while upgrades, resources, and enemy placements are randomized each time you level up. It manages to keep the sense of freshness that roguelites strive for, while avoiding the boring environments that are common with procedural generation. Weapons feel great to use, with each of them having unique mechanics. Progression feels good, and you're given control over when the difficulty of the game increases. You're also given plenty of control over how you specialize your build, despite the randomized upgrades that appear during expeditions, which act more as bonuses than important parts of your build.

There's a lot of attention to detail here, to the point where you can (and should) memorize which types of mushrooms will heal you slightly rather than damage or poison you. Be warned though that the game is fairly difficult. The Witch you're hunting will use every trick in her book to stop you, and at times your faith will be the only thing to save your skin.

Highly addictive game-play & loop mechanic. I'm not an FPS player but the RPG element and extraction possibilities make this a very good single-player game. It can be tough & there is a good grind to be had.

I really like this game, the combat and movement feels really good and rewarding, to me, movement is one of the most important aspects of the games I play, and this one achieves an amazing level of freedom at traversing the map.

There are a few things that feel kind of rough and that in my opinion could be polished in order to provide the player with better quality of life.

This game is difficult, it can be really challenging, but there’s a difference between difficulty and unfairness, those rough spots I mentioned are derived from the feeling of unfairness at certain areas of the game.

First, it can overwhelm you quite easily, you have to keep so many things and variables in mind that at some point you feel like you can’t just perform enough actions to save yourself, I’m talking about hordes of enemies just closing in on you from all sides, of course this is the objective the devs are probably trying to achieve and honestly, I think it is the right approach but here’s where some of the rough spots also show up the most:

- Enemies simply spawning behind you without giving you any hints until right before they attack, making it hard to plan and organize yourself with the environment 

- The poison mechanic, it is really frustrating when you are surrounded and trying to survive and you become poisoned from almost an unknown source without any real chance to fight it back, I really think this game would benefit from having a poison meter that quickly fills up instead of poison being an immediate status right after you get hit.

You don’t even have to get hit to become poisoned, just being close to a poison cloud is enough to immediately poison you, this becomes problematic when you can’t see the poison cloud but you still get the effect, and it’s even more problematic when you feel that you’re losing health just for existing in the world.

These are a few of the things that keep this game from being a truly challenging but enjoyable experience and turn it more into a challenging and frustrating experience with enjoyable moments here and there.

[h1]On the path of esoteric gunfights[/h1]

As a fusion of first-person shooter and dark fantasy, Witchfire blends roguelike and soulslike elements into an unforgiving battle for the life of your gothic sinner turned witch hunter. The moment you step into its cruel world, corrupted and twisted by witches and their hellish minions, your life turns hostage to the last couple of bullets in your revolver and the crumbs of stamina only enough for one last dash.

Where Witchfire truly excels is in its uncompromisingly challenging shooter mechanics, delivering combat where every shot is weighty and explosively satisfying. Even the starting revolver provides incredible pleasure from the recoil, the feeling of steel weight in the hand and the dull crack of an enemy’s skull being split. Of course, this isn’t enough to defeat the hordes of undead and other witches’ degenerates. They will swarm you and weaken you with madness. They’ll shoot bows and pelt you with spears, call in heavy halberdiers or musketeer squads whose marksmanship is no less than yours. Or even summon an entire ghostly galleon, hovering in the sky and shaking the entire level with the roar of its cannonade.

In order to progress, you’ll have to undertake raid after raid. Gather enough experience to level up, unlock new weapons and magic, and eventually gain access to new locations. The layered upgrade system, filled with meaningful choices, encourages exploration and experimentation.

Leveling passive skills is not the only way to get stronger. Seek quests — kill foes in different ways or under special conditions — and collect rare resources to unlock new weapon perks. Layer spells atop your arsenal, and witness unique combos emerge, where magic and gunplay entwine in unexpected symbiosis. Relics and artifacts, hidden across locations or forged in your sanctuary, add yet another depth to gameplay and open up various battle tactics.

Finally, you can raise your Gnosis level. It provides a deeper dive into an esoteric insight of witchcraft and hidden truths — stronger enemies emerge, new mini-quests whisper secrets to you, and challenges intensify. Simply speaking, Gnosis functions as a difficulty system tied to rewards and exploration. With every ascent, the prizes grow richer, and you unlock more areas, regions, gear, and gameplay mechanics.

Visually, Witchfire is a triumph, complemented by sound design, that heighten tension and immersion of this grim dying occult world. There’s no point in talking about it for long; you can only experience the beauty of this world by going on a witch hunt yourself, armed with a trusty shotgun and spells that burn everything in its path.

Combat is clear and responsive. Audio helps the player understand what is happening around them. Because of the hectic nature of this game Directional audio is important. Each weapon has a distinct way to use it beyond just the handling. Spells can be unlocked for some additional firepower. 

There is no story incentive to go to A > B > ... > Z (Fin). Instead as you play through each map you find things you can't access. Which hints you into doing something to grant you access. So it's much more about exploration, Which I love, and the experience of finding something new that keeps you moving forward. 

There are 3 types of progression in this Rogue lite game. 
Meta-Progression, Which have you unlock new guns, relics, Totems & Spells between each run. This Progression doesn't necessarily make you stronger but allows you to change your play style or find one that suits your particular skills. Some of these Meta-Progression you can unlock can be found mid-run. I am currently running a pure fire spell build, which under some circumstances can Mowe down hordes of enemies. But I started with using a more defensive ice build to slow enemies down giving me the upper hand. 

Story Progression.
Some of the Meta-Progression also unlocks new areas you can access, which helps paint the story of what has befallen the lands. In my opinion this is currently lacking. However it doesn't take anything away from the gameplay. 

Mid-Run Progression.
During a Run you find and fight a node of enemies. When you clear one of the nodes you are rewarded with a Giant Crystal. Which grants you 1 out of 3 potential upgrades of a specific type. The types available varies based on the equipment you chose for the run. If you have no way to do Fire damage you will not find a Fire based upgrade. These upgrades range from utility like an extra potion slot, to "Deal increased damage to Elite enemies". If you die or leave a run you loose these upgrades.

The combined above things keeps me coming back for more. I want to see what is behind Genesis 4, in the Pyre puzzle in the Spire of the Island of witches. The combat keeps me engaged. So I very much like this game.

I have a fair bit of experience in boomer shooters, especially the wave of modern ones, as well as a couple years in EFT and I've played Remnant for a little while. 

This game actually has delivered on all of the various tags so far; I'm not that familiar with Dark Souls specifically, but the rpg system has felt robust enough to make me want to start a bunch of characters, and still smooth enough that I didn't feel the need to pull up a wiki just to play the game. 

The stamina and health mechanics do a good job of making you commit to actions; I've seen some criticisms of enemy placement and stamina limitations, and I can't really agree. These games sometimes have the problem of over-mobility; it's fun to move fast, but past a certain threshold you become functionally untargetable, and so games like Doom Eternal have to turn up the enemy projectile speed and aggression to demand that you use the movement that way. That's fine if the entire game is built around that style of combat, but this game is an RPG, and so the choice to allow you to be quick without necessarily being generally fast, was a good one. Enemies have clear and distinct animations and timings, and while they can be unforgiving, that's only in the sense that you have to be patient and deliberate; if you're constantly dodging or sprinting, the enemy timings will eventually catch up with you.

I think this sort of design is something that games like Borderlands have always struggled with; balancing shooter mechanics in an RPG framework seems difficult, and this game (at least so far) has married the two nicely. I also like that you get sign posting, and a general progression, but the game is cryptic with a lot of information, so I did have a satisfying feeling of slowly discovering more and more complex layers to the game. The only concern I have is replayability; I don't know if the content currently in the game can support multiple long term (dozens to hundreds of hours) characters, like Dark Souls or Fallout, but so far it has stayed fresh and interesting. I'm curious what late game challenge looks like in this game, because I can see space for it to have depth, but traditionally that's one of the places where RPG shooters struggle, so we'll see. Heavily recommend.

Who is this for: fans of souls-like shooters like Returnal and Remnant, but want that top-tier tight gunfeel from Destiny 2. 

Visuals: Grimdark, dark fantasy, occult and gothic. Atmosphere is part Bloodborne, part Infinity Blade. Environments span from the remains of a castle atop battleworn ground to a dark tower overlooking a coastline hiding secrets to be discovered, and the violent tension is everywhere.

Gameplay: You explore, shoot and cast spells across several sandbox levels. You choose to push on and potentially die, losing all your resources to level up, or you run away to fight another day, level up and get back into the fight smarter and stronger.

Gunfeel, gunplay, and gun sound are top-tier and among the core foundations the game is built on. With every weapon allowing you to master its mini gameplay loop, for a more powerful output.

Enemies are a challenge, without being impossible. Often easily overcome with a mix of remembering their timing and moveset, and you optimising your build for DPS. Boss fights are pretty epic… but that’s for you to discover.

Sound design: Immersive. The foreboding music, the haunting drone of the winds, the chimes that make the back of your neck stand like Spidey-sense - could be a boon, could be a curse. The sound of pitter-patter of feet and the scream and growls of the occult around every corner. 

And then all hell breaks loose. 

Summary: This all coalesces into second-to-second tension, minute-to-minute action, hour-to-hour anticipation. You will die. And you will return, every single time, always, for one... more... round. 

Can't wait for 1.0. Where they actually flesh out the story.

At the time of this review the game is in early access and has had the Webgrave update released for just over 1 month. Review is subject to change depending on content added. 

The Story is very reminiscent of something like the Witcher while taking the approach of doing things in Fromsoft fashion with item descriptions and environment to tell the player the story which is a narrative style i do enjoy. There aren't really characters in this game except for notes but the game does a great job at focusing on the main goal rather than wasting time with exposition that would drag the experience down. 

The Settings are so well crafted and feel very lived in. I really like how each map that you can explore has many secrets that reward the player for exploration and dedication to leveling up and getting better at the game. Each zone within a map feels like a mini arena that offers a lot for players to explore and navigate during combat. It's very clear that the devs had a clear goal in mind and wanted to put out the best content that they possibly could. 

Visually, its gorgeous. Performance was solid for the most part with the newest map having some frame drops, but with this being early access and with the amount of updates and care that the devs give, this is only a minor hickup that will soon be fixed. Apart from that I didn't run into any bugs or glitches throughout my playtime. The Art Direction has this mix of both realism mixed in with a gothic aesthetic which i just love in games and definitely was one of the main selling points for me. It definitely feels very gritty which for a game like this is just the perfect vibe for the overall experience. 

Sound and Audio are on point with the soundtrack being really tense and mystical, keeping with the vibe of the experience and giving the player the right information depending on interaction. The Audio design is just so good as every weapon you wield feels like they pack a punch and even shooting enemies such as some of the armoured ones sounds great with the bullets hitting off metal. Its just a treat to hear and is great feedback. 

In terms of Gameplay, it somehow manages to take some of the best elements of different games and puts them into one experience without loosing focus. The movement and combat feels like its ripped straight out of Destiny which makes me feel right at home. The rogue-like elements are pretty cool, but its clear to see that this game focuses more on other aspects other than this. I'm not saying that its bad, but you shouldn't come into this thinking that this is a pure rogue-like. I think the extraction shooter elements are really well implemented and the game does a great job at making the player feel like they can loose all of their earnings in 1 run. Enemies are actually smart and will try to flank and use different abilities against you making difficulty interesting rather than making them bullet sponges. The guns, spells, items are all well varied and offer so much customisation when it comes to gameplay, even with the upgrades offering new playstyles which is just a breath of fresh air in the greater scheme of things. Finally, the boss fights definitely feel like they take inspiration to souls games and just feel great to go against. 

Overall, Witchfire prides itself on quality over quantity and I can't wait for what the devs have next in store for this game. Can't wait for it to be in 1.0!

I haven't played many extraction shooters, and this is the only single player one I've played, but Witchfire is fantastic. I'm actually really glad I jumped on the game while it was in early-access, because I see it blowing up in the future when it goes full release.

The setting and themes are dope, I love the gothic/Christian witch imagery and background. The progression is slow to start with, but satisfying over time. Once you start leveling up your Gnosis level (the world difficulty level system), you really start to see what the game is all about. 

If there are any negatives, it's that the game can be very grindy for sure. There are a lot of things to level up, and they can take some real time to get them there. Leveling your character is a good example, I'm just now level 50 after 24 hours of game time. I recommend upping the weapons first, they're your most significant source of damage for a while. Also, some spawns can feel unfair AF. Spawn in, open the map, see 4-5 skulls and traps surrounding your location, they proceed to fight for your life or dip out the portal you came through.

Overall, Witchfire is a banger and I'm glad I made the investment after having on the wishlist for quite a while.

Witchfire is a beautiful looking game with a VERY solid sense of progression. Difficulty is, in my opinion, well balanced and paced as far as a progressing curve goes. There is some nice variation here, too. Despite that fact, the gameplay will stay more or less the same throughout; which is to say you'll be shooting things perpetually for the entirety of the games duration, (not a bad thing for those of us that enjoy clicking on heads) however, the locations and weapons at and with which you will be doing said shooting are very nicely varied and have great depth.

The weapons, for example, each have their own unique personalities and behaviours, so to speak. what I mean by this, without getting into too many spoilers, is that the arsenal in this game is varied not just by model or make, or category of weapon. There is much more to them than just that. As an example, there is a firearm in the game that, after completing a certain amount of tasks and applying some upgrades, becomes a precision reload weapon, reminiscent of the guns from the Gears Of War franchise. As is true in GOW, hitting the precision spot during the reload will provide you with a bonus to your next fired rounds. Elemental effects and damage boosts, for instance. To speak to the degree of variety and uniqueness involved here, there are no other guns in the game that offer this same mechanical function. It is the only of its kind, and every other gun (of which there are many) is just as unique, with their own and layered mechanical offerings.

The maps offer a similar level of variation, also. They are procedurally generated, to a certain extent. Not geographically, mind you. It's more of a case of enemies and items being shuffled around, but only when the player ascends in level or uses in-game items to induce the effect. The maps themselves stay exactly the same topographically, meaning, thankfully, that they are hand crafted and designed from the ground up.  This results in some truly stunning locations and scenery with a great deal of atmosphere and a strong sense of exploration and rewards for doing it. To make up for the fact that the maps never change in the larger sense, the devs have given us a fair few of them. They are all quite large, and each has within them a 'dungeon' of sorts, which offers players great difficulties to overcome, and in turn, great rewards to earn for overcoming them. 

I'll leave this short review here to save from getting into any major spoiler territory, however, i will depart with some final words on the game for those still reading and debating on the purchase.

This is an extraction shooter-lite (you have to extract with your newly gained items and treasures in order to actually earn them), so if you aren't a fan of that genre, there's a chance it won't be for you. That said, I myself am NOT a fan of extraction shooters (I'd rather sit and rub a fresh hemorrhoid with sandpaper for the duration of a round of any extraction shooter than play one) and yet, here I sit, writing a fairly glowing review for this one. This, I believe, is because Witchfire somehow manages to avoid some of the frustrations inherent within the genre by way of mixing in some of the stronger elements from other popular games and their respective genres. As an example, we have some fairly obvious Souls-like mechanics here, the best of which being the borrowed death mechanic that allows players to return to their corpse and pillage some of or all of their lost items. There is also a heavier emphasis on Roguelike mechanics, which I happen to absolutely ADORE as a genre. There are also items that are bound to you, in the sense that they will not be lost upon death regardless of whether or not you return to your corpse. So, even if you disagree with the extraction genre completely, you may find yourself looking past or even enjoying it here. Much to the games credit. 

If all of the above sounds good to you, I'd STRONGLY recommend this game. In exchange for your money you WILL receive;

 - Plenty of value for money.

 - Amazing visuals.

- Satisfying, well designed gunplay.

- A real, difficult challenge that demands mechanical precision and decision making skills from the player, but is fair and reasonable in return.

- Fantastic optimisation (I'm running a decent rig with a 5090 and 9800X3D, but still, I've played on lesser hardware and it ran at more than acceptable framerates) with sturdy frames and a nice selection of graphical and other options in the settings menu.

Throughout my play I have continuously been surprised. If being "okay" is a death knell in the current gaming market place, Witchfire goes well WELL above that.

Gun play is solid, and each weapon feels unique, my only complaint would be the aggressiveness of the Calamity meter, it forces you to get better at the game, but it can be frustrating when you accumulate strikes against you without a clear indication of what you did wrong.

Ultimately, Witchfire is at its heart a soulslike, with a slight hint of extraction shooter.
Much like a soulslike, the class selection at the start just determines your starting stats and equipment. On death, you drop your belongings and need to recover them.
Pretty much most of the tropes you expect of a soulslike, you'll find here in an FPS format. 
The most unique aspects of the game, in my opinion, are the level design and the weapons. The game is split into a series of open maps, filled with secrets you have to find on your own. It is extremely compelling, and every map has a distinct layout and personality.
The weapons each have three tiers of progression, with each tier unlocking a core functionality of each weapon. Honestly, there are only two weapons I felt underperformed. All others were excellently-designed with unique niches and fantasies that are all useful and powerful. 
As far as critiques I could give, there aren't many. But there are a few key ones:
- There aren't enough bossfights in the game. Each map has a single named boss to fight. While it fits thematically, it does mean that there are only 4 unique bosses in the game as of writing, with at least 2 more still in development.
- The design ethos of the Calamity system eludes me. It is a system designed to punish you for taking damage by initiating an event in which you have to either kill a horde of enemies or destroy a circle of floating skulls elsewhere on the map within a time limit. In this game, healing is very limited initially, and enemies deal no small amounts of damage. So a system tacked on to punish taking damage even further seems a little... overkill, honestly. If there were a way to push back the calamity timer as a reward for finding secrets/performing well, I'd like it a little more, but as of now it's kinda a "kick the player while they're down" mechanic.

Overall, I found the game to be a lovely time with great gamefeel. What flaws this game does have are minor, and are already being worked on as part of Early Access. I greatly recommend!

Witchfire Webgrave Update

The game is now in a great place, even from what the devs are saying (for Q1 2026 1.0 and how the game now is almost mostly about more content) and Steam/Reddit agrees the game feels excellent to play and very polished. I said it before, but if you miss Destiny being Destiny - here's a witch-themed Destiny that replicates that signature of Destiny-Bungie-Halo like gun and movement feel. It's excellent, also because it's not just trying to be Slavic-Witcher-like Destiny, but also just having strong progression and game loop. It's just fun, the enemies are fun, the guns and upgrades are fun. Not to sound like a broken record, but it's all just fun. There's a nice mix of moods too, from more Slavic-Nordic elements to some Inquisition-style Spanish influence and a lot of western vibes straight from Hunt: Showdown.

There are not many games I would recommend in early access (like No Rest for The Wicked) because they feel too amazing to play (and have almost no bugs), but this is one of them. Early 2026 is not far off, but if you get in now - you have almost the final version. After 60h (20h of this new update), I'm level 81, so more-or-less late-mid/early-late game.

The roguelite.
The random run roguelite element is well integrated into the game design, allowing you to further customise your build per run. As with many great roguelites (like Hades), you can upgrade your character and gain access to more control over the random skills by choosing tier prefs (a bit like gods' trinkets in Hades for getting more types of certain boons). You can pick between beefing up your guns (like dash reload or bullet refunds on crits, etc.), your magic, or your life. It makes for a fun random skill system that can make each run different even when using the same core gear.

The extraction.
I feel that this is where many people hesitate, as extraction shooters are usually a bit more hardcore. While Witchfire is an extraction shooter, it is also a single-player game. Most extraction shooters feel more intense as you know other players are out there and may wait for you at the extraction. With Witchfire, that's not the case. The game has systems to keep tension high (like extraction portals guarded by enemies or calamities that work as a timer for you to not grind one map too long) - it's never as stressful as in a multiplayer game and works great within the lore of the world for you to get in, fight the evil witch's minions, and make your way out.

Some tips if you start:
- Level up your guns, they can have game-changing mechanics, so even if you don't love the gun on level 1 - by level 3/3 it may be amazing and super fun to use.
- Mix status elementals, the game allows you to mix more elementals than just obvious ones like Fire and Ice. All elementals mix - so a decay and lightning can produce more lightning, or a fire with lightning can produce a more rapid burn. Don't be afraid to mix - you don't need to (you can) just focus on one elemental.
- Experiment with your gear - one ring or a totem can change the way you play. One of my favorite rings is one that freezes enemies when they melee you and you dash - makes (all enemies, but especially) elites much easier as all enemies in this game have a melee attack and it can be a pressure off if you can freeze a stronger enemy to strike back or just reposition. They melee - you dash - they freeze - you crit-hit. It's poetry. Or how about electric shocks every time you dash after hitting an enemy?

With the Webgrave update - Witchfire is one of the best FPS games on the market, it's fun - has very satisfying combat and gunplay and just works. Oh yeah - it's also great on Steam Deck - had to add that hahah.

First of all, this is a single player game. No playing with friends, that is probably the only "bad" thing I've come up with so far but I can't really say it is bad because I can not imagine a way to make this multiplayer anyway so I won't consider that for the review.

The game has a very very wide range of spells and weapons that you can mix and thankfully now there are easier ways to get them upgraded quicker (shadow orbs seem to spawn more often, used to barely have one sometimes now i've some sitting on my inventory waiting for me to finish the current one).

The upgrade system of weapons is straightforward; kill enemies, get new power, use new power X times and kill X enemies, repeat. But the effects you get from the new powers get more and more fun for a lot of the weapons. Spells are just "hit X enemies with spell" which is honestly fine. Nothing convoluted, no need to rack your brains there.

Leveling works like any souls game, you kill enemies and they drop witchfire that you use to level up. Easy, but this will change the maps layout of events too which is a nice addition to not make this feel like routine.

The new stats are more obvious to what benefits you get from them, feel free to experiment a bit since there are stat reset items in the game. They also added beads which make nice interactions with stats and weapons to improve builds even further.

Again, this is in early access right now but so far it has been worth every cent I spent on it and more. If you want a first person shooter survival game where you burn the wicked and the heretic this will do.

I really love this game, been playing it everyday since i bought it, but i had already played it in an earlier build (the game only had 2 maps then). This game is hard and unforgiving most of the time so i'm gonna do a list of things that annoy me. Please don't feel like i'm hating on the game, it's cool af, i just wish some things where better.

 
Hermitorium: I will never understand why this place must be so large. I mean it's a mild annoyance, but having to run around the place looking for the merchant or having to go downstairs everytime i want to check the gnosis progress gets annoying with time. Also are there plans to make the training room more useful? The test dummy dies too fast, it only serves to check how much damage your weapon is doing and the magic colldown doesn't reset so theres not much to test there.

Overall design: When i first saw the teaser for this game 7 years ago i got a huge Darkwatch vibe from it (trashy Capcom fps from 2005), i thought it would be super goth and wicked looking but the goth aspect is very dilluted in my opinion. Like i reach Velmorn and find a secret sniper there, the sniper has a scope with a cross in the middle surrounded by rose thorn looking stuff, but the actual weapon has a blue and red paintjob mixed with a brown wood funiture... Sorry to whoever made it, but it doesn't fit well to the setting and that goes to the vast majority of the weapons. Ok, i'm fine with hailstorm having a snowflake for a crosshair, but does it have to look like it came from santa's arsenal? The only weapons i have that really fit the game for me are Nemesis, Striga, Hunger, Psychopomp and Koschei. Also i know this is a huge nitpick, but when you shoot striga and you see that mundane, simple wooden stake magically materializing inside the barrel it's kinda funny.

Builds: I'm overall fine with it, but i think the Chronoclast should be removed. Yeah i see it's like elden ring or ds3 and you need a consumable to reset your points, but this is an extraction roguelike, not a soulslike. If i have to select an incense, choose and upgrade my weapons and magic before a run, why are you limiting my ability to build the character before tackling a spcific boss? It's probably not happening, but what if the whole level system was removed and the stat buffs came from the chosen fallen prayer? i got that idea from first berzerker khazan and to me it makes much more sense since the game is a roguelike. You find the mask shards, upgrade the fallen prayers with witchfire and each prayer has a different set of buffs focused in stuff like magic casting, weapons, meelee, etc. I'm also gonna add that the most OP builds for this game involve the Arsenal atribute 99% of the time and even if you build for witchery you'll still need good weapon handling and ammo reserves because of the cooldown system. Yeah leveling witchery reduces spell cooldown but to me the cooldown for spells is kinda unnecessary and could be substituted by a mana bar. Every time you kill an enemy the witchfire that comes to you would recharge a portion of the mana, enabling you to cast more often. I don't think any of this will be changed because the everything would have to be rebalanced, but it would be so much cooler and would make the builds completely chage the playstyle depending on what you choose.

Cruelty: My final complaint will be towards the abusing nature of certain parts of the game. There are moments in which the game betrays your expectations and makes it super easy, but othes in which you are obliterated for absolutelly no reason. The familiar from iron gate for example, i killed that sucker almost hitless in my first try with 8 crossbow shots and Echo spamming, but for some reason the path for the optional miniboss from Scarlet coast has poison flowers in the ground that take too much time to disarm, a ton of enemies shielded by hard to destroy efigies and like if that wasn't enough theres mines that deal heavy damage at the end of the tunnel, all that for a pretty mid, easy miniboss at the end and you can even disarm all the poison flowers in the arena before entering... Theres tons more like when the game accidentaly groups 3 enemy clusters in one spot and it becomes almost impossible to avoid wasting all your elixirs and ammo, the ammount of enemies you have to kill for each encounter and the ammo you have to spare is stupid sometimes, enemies should drop ammo more often! OH and what about the wailing tower?? You expect me to run around the island of the damned everytime so i can get strong before entering the tower just to recieve TERRIBLE debuffs, waste all my resources and have to fight a super hard boss, all for what? a machine pistol and some profecies... Sorry that is SH*T, theres no nice way of putting it. The tower's floors are hard, the debuffs are way too bad, enemies are annoying, numerous and the reward is weak.

Final thoughts: i like and recommend this game, but the direction some things took are down right bad. That doesn't mean i'm not playing when 1.0 is out as i said i love it ever since i saw the first teaser, but to me it could be better in simple ways that i'm sure the devs are capable of making. My only true request? Please add different weapon skins and make it so i can change the skins at the gunroom. Doesn't matter if they're free or require stuff to unlock them, just make it goth and spiky and i'll be happy.

- a very wide array of firearms (>20 at the time of writing, havenÄt used all of them), ranging from revolvers to submachine guns, to snipers, even a stake thrower like in good old PAINKILLER - it's all there and nearly a guarantee that everyone finds weapons to suit their style
-a good armament of magic spells (which can also be leveled up, alsoe around 20 or so at the time of review), damage spells, stun, crowd control, everything covered to fit your taste
- a reasearch mechanic (great so far - i hope they maybe add some parts to it to make it viable for even mroe replayability, or maybe it's already there, haven't reached high enough level of unlocks to see the final stage and it's in active development enyway)
-the ability to give yourself different buffs to make some runs more doable (was very improtant for me and helpful to flatten the challenge curve many times -which sometimes spikes up noticeable between different levels and gnosis stages (raises enemy hp and xp gains, you pick when to apply it, but can never go back to lower rating) 
- good level design so far with , 5 levels as i write this, with more in development and some planned additions to existing ones, levels are small to medium size so far - you are able to move from one end to teh other in accepable time and also many little collectibles (which is a good thing, since even when you need to backtrack you might find stuff that you missed the first time)
- good graphics (to clarify for readers: I don't really care about this myself, but they might not be as super  high-res realisticly overwhelming like some new RPGS or other shooters, but hell, this is a FPS with mystical creatures withces and zombies, and everythign looks nice, the essence is in the action and overall it looks pretty good, the screenshots don't lie, it's solid and good looking) - performance is great with my rig, 32gb ram, rtx 3080 and a Ryzen 9 5900x.

I could maybe think of other points (ad maybe format this better), but this shuld suffice for now. 
All in all I can say, although I rarely buy new games and am very careful of Early Access Titles, I can wholeheartedly recommend this game in it's current state, it's already a solid experience and hopefully will only get better. If you can, grab it at a sale, and even for "full price" now in Early Access it's worth it in my opnion and very likely will be worth your while, if you found any of the listed attrivutes intriguing.

TL;DR.
If Dark Souls and Destiny 2 merged in the best possible way — you’d get Witchfire.
Incredible gunfeel, moody atmosphere, and endless replayability. Worth every cent.

 Gameplay

The shooting feels phenomenal — easily on Destiny 2’s level of precision and impact. Every weapon hits hard, and just firing feels satisfying.
Each gun comes with unique perks and upgrades, keeping combat fresh. The balance is perfect: no overpowered builds, no useless ones — you’re always just slightly weaker, which makes fights intense and strategic.

It combines Destiny’s silky-smooth gunplay with Dark Souls’ deliberate rhythm and risk–reward feeling. The result? Combat that’s both thoughtful and thrilling.

 Balance & Challenge

Witchfire keeps you alert at all times. You can’t just rush through — timing, movement, and cooldowns actually matter.
Bosses hit hard but fair, rewarding focus and adaptability. The game punishes carelessness but never feels unfair — it’s always your fault, and that’s what makes it fun.

 Visual Design

Absolutely stunning art direction. Even the base area looks beautiful — you just want to stop and take it in. Every environment feels handcrafted, detailed, and alive. The atmosphere is dark and oppressive, but not horror — just the right amount of tension.

Exploring

Exploration is genuinely rewarding.
Hidden doors, events, minibosses, puzzles, and those little glowing fireflies leading to loot — there’s always something new to find. The game constantly rewards curiosity and careful observation.

 Sound Design

The sound work is exceptional.
You can pinpoint enemies by footsteps, locate secrets through distant whispers, and feel the tension build through ambient noise.
Play with good headphones — it’s immersive on another level.

 Verdict

Witchfire blends Destiny 2’s perfect gunfeel with Dark Souls’ challenge and atmosphere.
Every system — shooting, balance, exploration, sound — fits together flawlessly.

It's gonna be a small non-comprehensive review. Basically I waited until I unlocked and fully upgraded every weapon in the game before I made my review. I spent a lot of time deliberating whether to give this a yes or a no. The gameplay is there, it's polished, it's responsive, the weapons feel unique and fun, even things I thought I would hate upgrading actually felt good to upgrade. And while I wish after unlocking all three levels of a weapon there was a way to sink more resources into it perpetually to buff the stats, performance, or unlock alternate visuals for your favorite weapons, what there is so far is good. It's acceptable.
But now we get to why I was debating giving this review a yes or a no.
The screen shake.
My God, the screen shake.
I don't know the mechanics behind it, maybe I just grew less tolerant of it, but the more I put into the game, the more frequent it seemed, and it's heavy, and it's impeding, it breaks immersion, it breaks enjoyment. These random "quakes" that just, I've never in my 30+ years of gaming understood how people could complain about motion sickness in a videogame until I played Witchfire. There were a couple times where screen shake got so bad it physically made me recoil and turn away to stop myself from feeling like I want to vomit. It's doing an absolute colossal disservice to the game and it's a lot. It's a lot to take, and it's a lot to overlook considering you end up fighting it to be able to enjoy what I genuinely believe to be one of the finest gunplays in any videogame ever. Like genuinely the way guns handle and respond feels more fun and addictive than gunplay in Destiny at its prime.

If I could give you a recommendation purely on gameplay, it's a 100% unequivocal yes. It might be hard at the start it might be easy, but you can gear and upgrade to acomodate for both in the way the system is now. 
If, however, you suffer from motion sickness, are bothered by screen shake, it's probably a no. Know what you're getting into and understand that this has one of the most egregious, invasive, unfun, counter-intuitive screen shakes ever implemented in any videogame to date. 

And if devs happen to check out reviews from time to time and happen upon this one. Please for the love of all that is good in the world, please, add a way to disable the screen shake as soon as possible.
(Also weapon paragon/ascension levels.)

After spending more than sixty hours in Witchfire, I can confidently say it is one of the most satisfying shooter roguelites I have played. Developed by a small team, it delivers AAA‑quality visuals and a deep gameplay loop. As a preyer, I hunt witches with forbidden guns and pagan magic, and the game lets me decide whether to pick off enemies from afar, study encounters tactically, or combine firearms and spells into my own brand of mayhem. I am a long‑range enthusiast, and the time I have invested has been rewarded with memorable head-shots and tense cat‑and‑mouse encounters across the game’s richly detailed maps.

The July 2025 Webgrave update is the most transformative yet. It adds a brand‑new region called Velmorne, a blighted town full of secrets and new enemy types. This update introduces the Rosary, a system of passive skills that lets me tailor my build and share configurations with other players. The Workshop has been overhauled so I can control the research path of my gear, and the old stat categories have been replaced with an RPG‑style system using Flesh, Blood, Mind, Witchery, Arsenal and Faith. There are also new Gnosis levels and a redesigned Ascension Shrine, with a special item to reassign points if I am returning to the game. Webgrave even adds a proper tutorial via a prologue level and an in‑game handbook. For snipers like me, the highlight is the Oracle, a new sniper rifle that can ignore walls. There is also the lever‑action Nemesis and the quest‑locked Koschei. These additions, coupled with the Rosary and refined stats, make character builds more rewarding and combat more tactical.

This update builds on March 2025’s Witch Mountain update. That patch added a sprawling descent into Witch Mountain, the game’s largest level to date, and introduced Fallen Preyers 2.0, semi‑autonomous allies, Shadow Orbs that offer high‑risk, high‑reward challenges, and a suite of new gear. Earlier still, the Ghost Galleon update in April 2024 added souls‑style classes, new Calamities, a Calamity meter that teaches you to avoid mistakes, and the Gnosis system that lets you slightly over‑level and unlock hidden paths. These patches show that the Astronauts team listens to feedback from us and continually expands their world. They released a huge update just two weeks ago and released an updated patch today on Aug 13!

[b]The maps themselves are masterfully crafted and gorgeous to look at and run through.[/b] Early regions like Scarlet Coast are a study in melancholy; broken flotillas litter the shoreline, a blood‑stained beach and an abandoned fishing village give way to a quarry. Irongate Castle radiates corruption with its foul aura, labyrinthine dungeons and three separate ways into the castle! Witch Mountain’s labyrinth requires careful navigation and is filled with traps and Fallen Preyer allies. Velmorne offers narrow streets, blighted courtyards and new enemies that will surprise even veteran players. Each level feels like a mini‑dungeon; they are semi‑open but interconnected, giving me multiple angles to line up long‑range shots or retreat when calamities hit. The design encourages exploration with hidden Vaults, Shadow Orbs, Witchmarks, navigation charts and events that reward curiosity and precision.

[b]Weapons and sniping mechanics are a standout.[/b] The game already features excellent marksman rifles like Hailstorm, which has the highest base damage of any non‑demonic weapon. Landing three consecutive critical hits refunds bullets to the magazine and, at higher upgrade levels, improves handling, increases zoom distance and even unleashes a freezing shockwave. However, misses reset the buff and there is a stamina cost for aiming, so disciplined shooting is essential. Hypnosis, another bolt‑action rifle, rewards patience by charging extra damage the longer I aim. Now, with the Oracle’s ability to shoot through walls, snipers can set up truly spectacular shots in Velmorne or Witch Mountain. Mixing these rifles with spells, for example freezing cones to control mobs or shockwaves to knock enemies back, enhances the sniping loop and stacks the damage. Even demonic weapons like Vulture and Hailstorm act as panic buttons or boss‑busting tools, but I find myself returning to precision rifles because of how satisfying the critical‑hit system is. Stack that with electrical shock on top of fire...the damage numbers roll...

[b]Visually, Witchfire is jaw‑dropping.[/b] The game uses advanced photogrammetry and post‑processing to build gorgeous semi‑open world levels. The developers took their photogrammetry pipeline beyond The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, shooting objects at high resolution, using drones for large scans and compiling tens of thousands of photos to create assets. They then optimized these scans so the game looks stunning without sacrificing performance. Details like natural dirt, weathering and unique compositions give each environment authenticity. Even after dozens of hours, I still pause to admire the sun piercing through ruined arches or the way light dances off wet stones in Velmorne.

Witchfire has evolved into an exceptional roguelite FPS. The developers have continually expanded the game with new regions, systems and weapons, and the Webgrave update addresses onboarding while giving veterans deeper build options. If you enjoy sniping or methodical long‑range combat in atmospheric, dungeon‑like maps, Witchfire will scratch that itch. My 60+ hours have flown by, and with the Rosary system, new maps, gnosis levels to unlock and the Oracle in my hands, I'm not stopping.
