OK, yes.  I can, VERY tentatively say, "Yes, I recommend."  However, I am having several complaints that I am not entirely sure will ever be addressed.  And so, I am going to make a list of gripes, likely get hit with a "jester award" or fanboy wrath, and hopefully give someone who isn't "diehard" some insight.  I will start with....I am NOT a "Souls fan".  Personally, I find the entire genre to be, essentially, "unnecessarily difficult as a means to artificially pad your game".  That isn't to say I haven't played and enjoyed some.  I'm just saying they aren't my "first pick".

First off, the "souls-like" tag is pretty fairly earned, though not as bad as it could be.  If that seems like a problem to you, if it makes you "nervous"...probably move on.  However, I never felt like my ire was aimed at a "tough enemy".  Instead, it was aimed at terrain placement, or inconsistent AI, or poorly explained mechanics.  The game punishes you...fine...very "souls like".  However, it's got enough annoying me without being shot through walls or my dash being stopped short because of a small obstacle that shouldn't even be noticed in a gunfight.  It's infuriating enough to round a corner and get mowed down in one blast, losing all your loot.  Now imagine losing all your loot because a skull on the ground "blocked" you.

In that same vein, the camera has "its moments".  While it hasn't been frequent, it has been frequent enough that I made note of it.  Usually because of said "terrain", but the camera has gotten stuck in something several times or otherwise "glitched out"...spinning around and shaking with no way to see anything.  Again, in the midst of a heavy fight...not something that should be happening.

Secondly, the "familiars" or whatever the "boss-like" characters are....specifically the one of the Island of the Damned...are infuriating.  Not specifically because they are "hard".  Fine.  However, their behavior is inconsistent.  Some runs I'll come across him, spazzing out in his corner of the map and as long as I don't hit him; he's fine.  Other times, I'll be in a fight, nowhere near him, and he'll come over and "get involved"...usually wiping me out because I'm getting hit from behind and not at "full health".  Please do something about this.  It's really annoying to be doing some casual farming run and suddenly "Grunthok the Flatulent" comes out of left field and vaporizes you when you weren't even fighting the damn thing.

Thirdly, I feel like health drops need to be slightly more frequent.  I can go entire expeditions and not have one health serum drop.  Most I have ever seen is in one run is three (which admittedly for that run was PLENTY).  Still, to open 7 chests, kill every bad guy on that main map, and beat "Grunthok the Flatulent" and not get one health drop...even with the pitiful 1% Arcana boost chosen...seems a bit stingy.

Perhaps, there are all manner of explanations within some aspect of the game I haven't found.  The point is, these things are not exactly spelled out.  I still don't fully understand how "mysteriums" work and where to farm those.  The dungeon is annoying the crap out me with Sanity being introduced and I'm not entirely certain I understand THAT mechanic; but it seems to basically be just another way to drain your health in a game that is already doing it plenty....which just seems asinine.

I do enjoy the game.  And I can certainly hop online and find all manner of walk-throughs and guides.  The gunplay is pretty solid and the different guns I've used have each had their charms.  I WANT to like this game.  It's acting like that antisocial kid, though, berating you and being a general jerk every time you try to get close.

Maybe, instead of a "dash"...we can get a "teleport".  Perhaps make one of the traits tie in to "ease of traversing obstacles" so that, for instance, more mobile characters don't have small obstacles blocking them.  Give us more control over how "challenging" or "casual" we want a run to be (perhaps toggle if we want the extra bosses...and therefore extra loot chances....we've already beaten to be there on a certain run).  I saw another review mention tying calamities more into the loot you pick up and I can get behind that.  As it is, the game seems to either "kick you when you're down" or "let you roll over it".  "Feast" or "famine".

...And could we play "dress up" with our "Preyer"?  Sure, he looks badass; but, some customization would be "badasser".  Perhaps it's later and I haven't gotten there, yet.  I like making my character my own.  Sue me.

I really hope things get smoothed out on here because I am worried these issues I have will only get worse as I progress and fights get tougher.  I'll be PRAYING for the days that "Grunthok the Flatulent" was inexplicably getting drawn into fights a quarter map away; as I now curse "ZorZlub the Incontinent" for somehow nuking me across the map with a melee attack or something.  There is so much here and so much that COULD be here.  I just hope it doesn't end up alienating me and others before it can get there. with silly overlooks and mistakes.  As it is, while I can recommend it...I'm uncertain how long my own patience will hold out.

Edit:  I felt it was only fair to address my gripes with additional play time and research.  Firstly, I should NEVER [i]have[/i] to look up walk-throughs and forums for your game.  Much love and appreciation for the community that has stepped up to fill this gap; but, it was a task that the developer should have taken on.  This is a serious oversight.  There needs to be better explanation within the game.  Many of my complaints stem from the game not being clear about something and you either have to figure it out yourself or hope someone else has and is willing to explain it.

However, eventually, things do start clicking into place and, if you are willing to...the game is "eventually" a lot of frustrating fun.  Just be prepared, it almost feels like the first few stages and ascensions are nothing but a hazing.  The early game doesn't feel "right".  The "Gnosis" levels are the biggest walls and it isn't until Gnosis III and beyond that things seem to "normalize".  At least, that's how it was for me.  It wasn't until this point that things like "healing potions" began dropping with any frequency (though still, some runs, I'll have NONE......HOW?!) and my character has access to a mostly full compliment of abilities, skills, and weapons.

That's the biggest takeaway for me....this is a game that requires you to put the time in to experience it's best.  I'm 40 hours in an I still have only a "solid" grasp on everything (and there is still Gnosis IV and all that comes from that for me to learn).  I can say that, yes, small issues compound so if there is something that annoys you early that's a legitimate issue (say, the terrain posing serious problems)...it will only get worse as the hordes get nastier and bigger.  However, if you are willing to educate yourself a little and put in some extra work...this really IS a solid game.

Witchfire has some of the most satisfying combat in an FPS period; The mixture of a large variety of equipment, good movement + gunplay systems and enemy variety make combat something to look forward to; Everytime I went up a Gnosis I was excited because it meant more combat with a larger variety of enemies with more interesting designs and increased difficulty. My elevator pitch for Witchfire's combat is often "Like playing Destiny without having to suffer playing Destiny" as the gunplay and movement just feel so damn clean and as you gain levels, gather more equipment and upgrade that equipment you keep reaching higher and higher heights of how good the combat in this game can be. 
Expanding on equipment there is plenty of it to fit all different kinds of playstyles and to allow you to adapt to different circumstances. Every single weapon, spell and accessory in the game is unique. No weapon simply just fires bullets, no spell simply shocks enemies, no accessory simply gives you a shield; They all have unique gimmicks that you upgrade through repeated usage of those specific items like one of my favorites, the Cricket, which is a SMG with a low magazine capacity but high rate of fire sound like a pretty bad combo until you level it and gain it's gimmick of dashing after a kill reloads the magazine turning it into a mob shredding beast of a gun that is so damn fun to use.

Visually this game is simply breathtaking, I do not have the best of PCs and so I play on medium settings for the most part and even still Witchfire puts many AAA games to shame with how even on medium the lighting, the effects, the environments themselves all come together to produce such a visual marvel, if you look at my screenshots of Witchfire you'll understand immediately and if visual depth and good art direction are what draws you into a game world then you'll be living in this one. 

My only major criticism of Witchfire is that some areas can feel kinda hollow, Witchfire is still an early access game so this can be forgiven and they are actively adding new content to the game but for some areas in the game I wish there was more big events or particular reasons to run one map over another. 

Overall if you like games with tight gunplay, plenty of build customizability, amazing visuals and lots of replayability you're going to love Witchfire.

It's really hard to categorize this game.  It is a: First Person Shooter, an Extraction Shooter and a Rogue-like.  But it's also sort of adjacent to all of these categories.  You are a Preyer, a sinner who serves the Church by hunting witches, seeking redemption for their unforgivable deeds.  You travel through portals to different areas, filled with different enemies and scourge all that you find.  As you kill enemies, you gain currency/exp which you drop upon death, requiring a return visit to reclaim your lost witchfire.  If you survive and manage to return home, you may spend your witchfire to level up.  So, technically rogue-like with extraction elements.  I dislike the souls-like tag, as people tend to slap that on anything with a steep learning curve and tough difficulty.  But aside from losing your witchfire, there's no real punishment for death.  The fresh enemies that face you as you attempt to retrieve your "souls" are merely more currency and practice.  So I really am kind of stumped explaining this one.

Gunplay and spells feel super satisfying, and all builds are viable.  I ran a pistol wielding gunslinger with ice spells, dashing into combat and clicking heads, and then I ran a shotgun and summon build.  Guns are leveled up by killing enemies, revealing new abilities for each one that drastically change how you play.  One of the machine guns shields you with divine wings while aiming, allowing you to tank a free hit every 5 seconds or so, while one of the pistols rewards headshots and a shotgun rewards firing during a combat slide.

The game also features a "difficulty" setting called Gnosis.  As you raise your gnosis, the witch (the game director) is given a larger bag of enemies, enemy skills and traps she can use against each of your expeditions into her world.  This is re-rolled each time you level up, so sometimes you may face waves of shield bearing enemies and exploding traps, while another run may be filled with minibosses.  But enemy HP never changes!  So it's purely a challenge, rather than damage sponge.  Raising your Gnosis allows you to reveal hidden items in the world, research new weapons and equip more upgrades in addition to vastly increasing the currency earned in each expedition.

A quick word of warning: until you learn how the expeditions and enemies work and how events like Calamities impact the world, the game can be pretty tough. I got hooked after I learned the combat dance and how to exploit enemy attacks, which made me feel like the witch needed to fear me, rather than the other way around.  It's hugely satisfying to dodge melee attacks, executing the undead at point blank range, knowing a single misstep means I lose a chunk of health.  When you can pull it off, you feel awesome.  

As a side note, the devs are really responsive and post regularly about their thought process patching and changing the game. 

It's been an excellent experience and I highly recommend Witchfire.

I really, really like this game. I love that it doesn't hold your hand and but also doesn't unfairly punish you. I haven't died once and thought it was BS. It was always something I knew I did wrong. I got careless, I didn't notice a trap, I wasn't cautious enough. Learning the mushrooms and which ones heal and which ones harm was actually a super simple but nice mechanic. And if you eat a bad mushroom, it may mark a calamity point which nears you to a calamity event. I love how chaotic calamities feel. I like the rush to either get out or fight your way through it. When it hits and you notice you're low on ammo, or no healing elixirs really triggers flight or fight.

Enemies are nice and varied. Obvious grunts are obvious. Elites feel powerful and dangerous. I absolutely love when grenadiers shoot their mortar strikes and you see their shots volley way up in the air and crash down near you. It has a truly apocalyptic feel.

The world story telling is fantastic, the aesthetics are beautiful and wonderfully gothic. The world feels previously lived in and you get a feel for what the areas were like when there was still life.  The audio is also fantastic. Weapon sounds are impactful and full of little details like metal on metal sliding or clicking when inserting a magazine. Reload animations are also very detail oriented. Example: if you empty your shotgun, the first shell you put in is in the receiver, then you slide the receiver closed, flip the gun and insert shells in the loading port. So if you empty your gun, it takes slightly longer to load than if you loaded before it was completely empty. Also means loading one shot and firing is much slower than letting a couple shells load first. Shotguns are the only weapons I've noticed this with but I really liked that attention to detail. It's also very nice that all the feedback and information you need regarding buffs and gun mechanics are all animated on the gun. For example, the Angelus rifle, when your shield is ready, the glyphs glow. When you take a hit, it blocks it, amps up your damage by a lot, lowers your fire rate for increased accuracy and ammo preservation. While this is in effect, your glyphs glow really bright. When it's done, they go dark and then after a few seconds, the glyphs start to glow starting from the barrel to the trigger showing it's charging. 

The weapons and how you unlock their progression is also perfectly fresh. It forces you to use them, get comfortable with them, then unlock the first feature on it and then you have to use that feature x amount of times to unlock the next stage. Then finally do that one more time to fully unlock its full potential. The upgrades are meaningful and actually exciting to learn. The Duelist revolver for example, took some learning but now it's my favourite. At first, it's a normal revolver. After killing 25 enemies, you unlock the first upgrade. Now when you kill an enemy, it glows. Then you aim down sight, shoot an enemy once and the world briefly goes into slow motion. There's a varied amount of time in this slow motion until the hammer clicks and the barrel glows. At this moment you need to get a critical hit like a head shot or weak point, then it overpowers the gun for 4 or 5 seconds. The next unlock adds burn damage and decreases reload speed substantially while overpowered. The final upgrade extends the overpower duration for each enemy killed. There are 20 primary/secondary weapons to unlock and upgrade and 3 non-upgradable demonic special weapons. Special weapons have very limited ammo but are very powerful. 

I highly, HIGHLY recommend this game if you're into extraction shooters. There's a lot of love that's gone into this and runs can change fast if you make too many mistakes. Like I said, a bad mushroom can trigger a calamity, spawning a horde of demons to hunt you while your sanity meter ticks down until you either kill a number of calamity enemies or an elite spawned by the calamity, find your way to the calayst and destroy the skulls flying around it, or ditch and sprint your way to the nearest exit portal. I will say, that run when you're out of ammo and healing elixirs and carrying a ton of Witchfire, is exhilerating.

GOOD, but PARTICULARLY if you're into the VAGUE / DIFFICULT mechanics of the game.

PROS:

- Beautiful graphics, was running well on a 3070 ti / 9700x @ 1440, mostly 100fps with high setttings.

- It's true, people say it's Destiny2'esque in terms of core gameplay/shooting and it feels like a good clone here. The movement and shooting feel tight and responsive. Jumping is also high and floaty. Shooting and on-hit FX look spectacular once you get the right items and the SFX are very satisfying as are many of the weapons.

- Gameplay loop is decently addictive in a good way.

CONS:

- The pricing and content ratio is NOT there. This is a highly repetitive game with (IMO) very satisfying core gameplay. You will repeat the same similar runs very often right from the start. 

- You can only carry 2 main weapons with a 3rd powerful that has limited ammo. At the start, your character is weak; low stamina, health, low ammo, limited arsenal, no special items, etc, and you have to put in a fair amount of playtime just to build up to what many other games already start you out with. From there, you'll realize you're basically playing a numbers game with stats. Yes you WILL get to a point where there's a lot more going on as enemy count increases with difficulty as well as map events, how often you can dash, having more ammo, etc, but you'll quickly realize the game is very much about the grind but lacks the content-depth of other games at this price range, and FPS category. I think the GREAT core gameplay really carries the weight here. 

- Vague mechanics:  I keep referring to Google for things the game could explain to you but I one might argue that the mild vagueness adds to the mystery/fun in figuring things out yourself, but some things could stand to use an explanation.

- Adding to the above, in case you aren't aware already: the game is difficulty and quite unforgiving at times. I'd argue that it's more difficult at the start and it took me quite a bit of hours of gameplay to finally get to a point where it really falls upon your skill and things start to feel fair. 


At the end of the day, I still come back because of both the somewhat addictive gameplay loop & mechanics but I think most gamers out there looking for something with a bit more purpose & additional content might find the game to be VERY repetitive and shallow. Allowing for stat arrangements and so on with a small set of maps and enemies (IMO) doesn't really make up for a somewhat small amount of content, and you'll be repeating the same maps over and over again (with different playstyles) before you move onto the next.

I have played through witchfire to it's entirety. Gotten all the achievements and conquered the current witch mountain. I am only missing a handful of items in witch mountain because the progression kind of falls off the rails in there. I've done all of the timed dungeons at least once and killed every boss. My character as it stands is level 75. My criticisms mainly revolve around pacing and leveling which are the two biggest offenders that I can think of. Nonetheless, these criticisms clearly aren't dealbreakers for me as you could probably tell from my completion status.

On the topic of pacing. The Gnosis levels are a topic that I'd like to address. Once you hit around Gnosis 3-4. There's no new content in the form of weapons, spells, relics etc. The weapons system in this game hit struck such a chord within me that I was practically salivating at the thought of leveling up. I wanted to explore more and see what secrets the mirror was hiding. Only to realize the harsh truth that this game metaphorically blows its load with weapons too soon. There's no shortage of guns in this game. But you will have about 85% of them by Gnosis 3 with the rest being unlocked from miscellaneous things and exploration, not research anymore. There are 6 total Gnosis levels. My enthusiasm for leveling Gnosis quickly waned as the rewards became a very slow trickle. Only a small boost in witchfire earned along with new 'secrets'. Leveling up to 5 and 6 only lets you open a single odd door or two and nets you access to witch mountain. I don't consider those concrete rewards. Not in the slightest. The rewards for the lower levels of Gnosis are staggering compared to the higher levels and open the game up a lot more.

Next, on the topic of leveling. I have some gripes with how fast levels come. To begin, lets talk about witchfire. The leveling currency like souls would be in the dark souls franchise. Of course, when leveling. The amount of witchfire you need per level increases ever so slightly. The problem is not the increase in required witchfire to level up. The problem is acquiring witchfire. As mentioned before with Gnosis, you get small boosts in obtained witchfire as your Gnosis level increases. Each map you travel to also boosts its given witchfire with it's increasing difficulty level. Makes sense, harder content gives greater rewards. But as you play, you will notice that even if you clear out an entire map including killing it's boss at the very end. You will only have enough witchfire for a 1-2 levels maximum. I understand that there's a way to get millions of witchfire from a single run. Even the devs have championed these people showing "LOOK HE GOT 1 MILLION AT THE END OF A SINGLE RUN, THE LEVELING SYSTEM IS FINE." But that's simply not an accessible way to actually progress due to the huge drawbacks of using the items that give you more witchfire. Namely the foul stimulant item which heavily reduces your maximum health and stamina. At anything less than 40 flesh you will get 1-2 shotted. At anything less than 40 blood you will only have 1-2 dodges. To demand near perfection from players just to obtain levels in a reasonable amount of time is absurd. Especially when if you die after using the foul stimulant. You lose everything. This hardcore leveling system predominently benefits the already extremely strong player. The players who have enough to take the huge HP and Stamina hit and shrug it off. As well as nearly instantly clear any encounters they come across. That is where the millions of witchfire come from. if you don't believe me. The person who posted their million witchfire run claimed to already be around level 440-480. At that point, you don't need levels at all compared to players like me at not even level 100. But in order to comfortably grind I'm expected to do what they do? I expect anyone reading this to understand how absurd that is.

Rogue-lite shooter in a dark medieval fantasy setting pitting witch hunters with a religious background against the evil Witch and her abominations. Movement options include sprint, crouch, (double) jump and dodge making the Preyer feel pretty flexible while navigating forests, islands and castles. Depending on what you want to do in a run you can spend anywhere between 10 and 30 minutes on a map before returning to the Sanctuary hub area.

There's a level system for your typical RPG stats (Ascension level) as well as a meta-level system (Gnosis level) that increases difficulty as well as gained currency. The latter also changes what events and enemies can be encountered and what secrets can be uncovered and is directly related to meta / story progression. Then there is a passive ability system, represented by equippable Rosary Beads you can find scattered around the maps, that can net you important bonuses depending on your leveled stats. New equipment is unlocked by leveling up Gnosis to make it available for research first and then spending time on a map and eliminating enemies. That's a lot of different progression systems you're playing around with at the same time but they all play into each other so well that they still make up a coherent progression journey.

Every weapon in your arseneal feels completely different from the others because of their unique abilities. It's easy to see how much care goes into creating new weapons and explicitly making them feel distinct from everything that's already there. And with three unlockable levels per weapon - and some levels not just increasing the previous level's ability but adding completely new ones - there's a lot of variety here.

Reading Witchfire's devlogs a few years after seeing the trailer at The Game Awards long ago, I felt confused that they were eager to make this game as a Destiny-derived roguelite.

Having finally played the game, I'm confused that they were eager to make this game as a Destiny-derived roguelite.

What caught my eye about the first trailer was, simply put, that the sell of a shooter with souls-y presentation and mechanics felt like a novelty in the genre. High-damage enemies that have to be consciously dodged, high-impact weapons, high-caliber environments and level design, you know- something that evokes that on-edge feeling of exploring something grand and dangerous, where it's satisfying just to progress. 

Witchfire still has some of that going on, but it feels blunted by the other aspects of its design. The very obvious affinity held for Destiny is especially confusing to me, as Destiny, to me, feels almost diametrically opposed to what a good Fromsoft-styled game can offer, where even normal encounters are consistently engaging. Gunfights in Destiny often feel more like pulling weeds than having a gunfight, and honestly, it's often the same here. You have battles with fodder that are utterly mind-numbing and THEN it throws something real at you and if you're sleeping at the wheel and die there, you have to deal with a ton of fodder again by virtue of the roguelite structure, and every time you return to a level after leaving it to save your not-souls. 

The game's art in general is gorgeous, the alt-colonial dark fantasy setting is neat, but while playing I just kept wishing that the game was a more traditional singleplayer game where individual battles and explorations felt meaningful as opposed to things that would be revisited without much joy over and over again. 

I'll note in fairness that I didn't get far in Witchfire, around two hours- but there was no point in those two hours where the game really clicked for me and I went "oh, now it's getting fun." I did hear that the game was made significantly easier between its initial launch on Epic and its launch on Steam, and I wonder if I would've liked it more back then- or perhaps the opening levels were always this way. Either way, I am interested in checking out the game again at some point, maybe when it's done- but likely with very different hopes.

Witchfire is a visually stunning game with gorgeous artwork, atmospheric environments, and a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack. Unfortunately, that’s where my enjoyment ended.

The enemy density is surprisingly sparse, leaving large stretches of gameplay feeling empty and unengaging. Magic, which should have been a standout feature, feels underutilized and limited, playing second fiddle to the gunplay. Combat leans heavily on dodging and fast reactions, but the high lethality makes this feel more punishing than rewarding.

Weapon damage falloff forces you into close quarters far too often, turning most encounters into frantic scrambles rather than tactical fights. For a game that promises variety and supernatural power, it funnels you into a narrow playstyle that quickly grows frustrating.

Witchfire is a case of great presentation let down by uninspired and unforgiving gameplay.

I can sort of see the appeal, but absolutely not for me.
My issues:
1. The gameplay/run-n-gun loop has too many flow breakers: your first gun has a cold/hot/overheated state, but if you drop ADS, that resets. So you have to keep ADS up and firing. But it's also a super weak assault rifle that has to be reloaded all the time, so again - balancing that "hot" state feels needlessly fiddly. It's not impossible, just not very fun - kind of like trying to remember a slightly confusing schedule of when you have to take your bins out.
2. Healing is garbage: one health item, that doesn't fully heal you, and ALSO takes you out of the combat flow state to use? No thanks... Estus Flasks this isn't.
3. In-level perks are almost all garbage with a few exceptions, and the "see a third" material drops seemingly at random with no way to get some before you've already gained some perks. I don't really understand why it's even there
4. Enemies are pretty basic with a lot of homing attacks that while they aren't impossible to dodge, add another layer of annoyance on top of the flow-breakers above: if I'm facing an aquabus guy, for example, I have to shoot him; then break LOS to dodge the magic bullet he fires, then rub marmalade on my gun to unlock a 12% damage buff, then fire a few more bullets, reload (which interups Dodge), then change the oil on a 1980 Ford Escort to trigger my Marzipan Spell buff... and I found after a while I really didn't care.
5. Bosses are just random hit-spam nonsense - doesn't feel like Dark Souls where I can go defensive for a few runs to learn a pattern, then juice up and counter punch them. In this I just sort of have to hope I don't die and that I've got enough bullets and cranberry poptarts
6. WAAAY too little ammo for a game where the melee is time locked AND I'm forced to use a crappy full-auto SMG. I was dry half the time because I went to punch a low health guy but I hadn't waited the requisite 4-6 weeks for my punch to go from Anaemic Slap With A Herring to Actual Punch.

It probably will get better, the art is lovely, and the Devs obviously seem to care, but I just didn't get into the flow or the gameplay loop at all. I had a few massively successful runs and a few stupid deaths and I felt like I played the same each time

Witchfire is very Dark Souls-esque in its gameplay and level of basic difficulty. You are given a basic tutorial and thrown into the deep end, with enemies that are too strong for you, ready to fight even in the prologue. You are left to find your own way through your various expeditions, with no guarantee of a safe path to your destinations, and no checkpoints to pick you back up where you croak (and you will croak).

Some people find that game style fun. If you're one of them, I actually would recommend giving this game a try. There's a neat story brewing wrapped up in a very well-realised world that offers a lot of exploration and a steep survival challenge.

I play games to relax and I don't find that particular style of play relaxing. If you're in that same boat, you probably won't enjoy this one.

The sound and visual design is really appealing.
The gun play and movement also feel really good but what I use them for doesn't.
The game just feel kinda disjointed. As if the maps weren't made with the movement in mind. But the movement feels as though it was made with the combat in mind.
Personally not a fan of the "camps" of enemies. The areas in between feel empty and the camps themselves just function as little arenas.
With how the enemy encounters and combat is designed, I would have enjoyed it a lot more in enclosed environments similar to something like Gunfire Reborn so that if I wanted to keep combat going I didn't have to trek around for it.
I also expected the "loot" to be loot, and not just resources.
Also clearing the first map of enemies, getting to the tower and opening it, then being unable to interact with the "final" thing of the map because I hadn't hit the progression point for it felt really bad. Also having to back track for an exit after realizing I had nothing left to do felt super boring and discouraging.

From the small experience I had with the game, I would not recommend it for the price.

Witchfire is a really weird game. I think the word I would use is that it feel directionless, and has no spikiness. The pitch of "FPS Rogue/Souls-like set in a dark fantasy world hunting witches" is right up my alley, and I was ocassionally looking at the dev logs, but like... it just doesn't work? And I don't really understand what I'm missing that so many people seem to adore about the game.

I'll note up here, right now, the performance of the game is really, really WEIRD. It runs at 120hz for me (3080, 3850x), but it's so jittery. Sometimes I open a menu and the game freezes for multiple seconds. The game drops frames and hitches constantly, sometimes up to 1-2 seconds at a time. It's not quite unplayable, but it's super noticeable and you will have to ignore it if you want to play more. I'm not sure what it'd run like on worse hardware, but if it's more jittery, it was already pretty close to intolerance for me.

But spikiness. What I mean by spikiness is, think of Tarkov. The difference between a TOZ-106 and a HK 416 is gargantuan. If you're sneaking around with a TOZ, get the drop on someone, and grab their rifle, you feel like a god, but also this massive sense of anxiousness until you get out safe with it. Gunfights are short and brutal, and every shot could be lethal. You open a cache, and you know that it could contain something worth millions. There's these spikes of fun.

Think of Hades. The difference between your power at the start of a run and the end is massive. You're whizzing around leaving blades everywhere and lighting is coming down and your gun now shoots five grenades and the bullets track enemies. Your difficulty can also increase so you have to absolutely perfect the game to get under time and not get hit. Spikey.

Think of Dark Souls or Elden Ring. That moment of "Oh shit what is that fucking thing" or "Oh cool a new weapon, oh it looks cool" or "Finally, I can upgrade four levels of my weapon and dump on enemies". The spikes of joy at finding a chest, or beating a boss.

Witchfire is bizarre because it feels like it has no spikiness. When you kill a camp of enemies, you get a level-up and a buff! But the buffs are all boring; do you want +20% stamina? +3% damage per 10% of your health you're missing? Perhaps +1 potion slot! They're all so... dry and mundane. I unlocked four weapons, and they all felt like they killed enemies at roughly the same rate, in roughly the same way; point at the head and pull the trigger. You would think the shotgun would be so much more effective since it's close range, but it just kinda wasn't? I upgraded a weapon; it does ~50% damage on undamaged enemies, so on the first shot! Yay?

Like there's this strange lack of joy in the game's meta existence, and it feels like there's a bunch of alpha-level cool mechanics, but none of them really come together to form a whole? The movement feels great, but I never really feel like I need to or should move much (and you run out of stamina REALLY quickly). The guns feel solid and kinetic, but they all do kinda pitiful damage; my bolt action takes 2-3 headshots to kill the weakest enemies, I can't imagine what the automatics feel like. They also have really weird range; damage drop-off from range goes to basically zero, and it's not like at 100m, it's closer to 10m using a revolver.

There's portals you can use to leave the map, and there's a timer! Oh no, you'll have to... stand there and do nothing because it doesn't trigger enemies or anything. I found a key, I can go use it to open up that chest I found, and it.... has some ammo and 2 pieces of gold? Ok? I came back from a run, so now I have enough to level up! I can buy one skill level. Ok, are they meaningful? I mean... you can get +3% stamina! Or perhaps +2% more money. Or +10% health?

Like I can't quite explain this properly if you haven't played, but it just felt like everything was kinda a dissapointment the moment I unlocked it, and that left me with no drive to see more things. Like every moment the game had to go "Look at this cool new thing! One more run to test it out maybe?" or "What an amazing find; what else could be out there?", it just threw me a couple coins and told me to fuck off. 

I dunno. It's kinda bizarre. Maybe if I played a couple more hours the game completely opens up and it suddenly gets better? I stopped because I got inside of the first tower, and the game told me that I didn't grind enough to progress, so I went back home, and it told me that I needed to grind more to progress. The game doesn't feel like unsavable or like a mess, it just feels like at least to me, none of the parts fit together in a fun way? I have to imagine after this long, this is the feeling the dev wants in the game, but I just can't really see why. Like taking a tiny case study; is the emotion I'm supposed to feel after finding a chest, not being able to open it, finding a key, and going back to open it confusion at what I got, and a sense of "Oh I guess it's more than it's sounds like?", only to go back to base and realize, no, it is indeed pretty much meaningless? Is that the intention? Because it really permeates every element of the game.

I like PVE extraction, I'd heard some neat things about how this changed up the genre formulas, so I tried it. But, ultimately every choice it made to be different, made it boring. Ultimately, it's just not as fun as any of the things it's inspired by.

What I enjoy from these kinds of games is them offering me a palette of abilities, items, routes, enemies, upgrades, and weapons that i can have fun trying combinations of. If an experiment doesn't work out, that's ok, death is part of the game and it should invite you to try something new - you should feel like you're the one setting the goals, because you want to do something cool or try something different, even if ultimately the designers are the ones who carefully put those opportunities into place.

This game just doesn't do that.

It's "extraction" in the original sense; you find and extract with souls that you use to make permanent progression. Like Hunt or a bit of Division:DZ. You're not getting Tarkov here, with hundreds of items to sift through and consider - you're really just picking up souls. Alright, but the things you spend it on are fairly inconsequential - stamina, health. You research weapons, you upgrade them by completing challenges, but you never really lose anything -- just the souls you were carrying at the time.

I've called it souls, because really, it's souls. You have a few perks you'll find that are reset each raid, but the thing that gates you is dumping souls into levelups and weapons. 

You might say "ah, so it's soulsey in that they enemies are also difficult and rewarding, right?" Well, no. Even the trash mobs are [i]spongey[/i], they have huge telegraphs but they hit very hard. There's no chip damage in this game, if you get killed it's probably because something absolutely postholed you into the ground because you missed a dodge. The game doesn't reward you for moving, shooting, cutting sightlines, and managing enemies -- it rewards you for holding m1 on them for a very long time, and pulling off perfect dodges. Is this "difficulty?" It doesn't feel like it. In Souls games, the difficulty evaporates once you figure out an enemy - you can punish their weaknesses and beat them quickly once you get what you're supposed to do. Here, the challenge seems more to be a test of patience.

You might say "well, you only played an hour, maybe the fun comes later". Maybe it does. Best of luck to you in searching for it.

Witchfire, on the surface, seems like it should be a lot of fun. The idea of a PvE extraction shooter with the grit of a souls-like sounds really appealing! But in reality, this game just doesn't deliver a FUN experience, and ultimately, doesn't respect the time of the player.

This game has a serious issue with how it handles it's progressions, taking way to long to feel worthwhile, especially in the early game. There's no reason why I should be playing this single player game with the same starting loadout for 3 hours. It takes AGES to unlock anything new, being tied to 'Real Time' timers, which I'm sure is fine if you like to drown all your time into a single game, but for someone like me, it's frustratingly slow and unsatisfying. If any game that you play has the caveat that it gets better after "x" amount of hours, then it's just not a good game.

Witchfire also feels like it missing a core mechanic that all the souls games have (and the vast majority of extraction shooter for that matter), which is online gameplay. It's a lot easier to get lost in a game for hours on end when you've got a friend to play through with, but instead your slogging through the first couple areas by yourself while you wait for things to unlock. It just feels like a gaping hole in the gameplay, and with the developers staunchly against it, it feels like they're gimping themselves. Much like the souls games, I don't necessarily think it needs to be primarily a multiplayer game, but having the option of co-op would do the game a lot of good in the long run.

On a positive note, I think the visuals and atmosphere of this game are awesome. Artistically this game does everything right, from visuals to sound design. It's obvious they had a lot of skilled artists on their team. It's a cool premise with a lot of SICK visuals, and everything works together to really sell the vibe this game is going for 100%. It has the exact kind of dark gothic vibe that you would want from anything that carries the souls-like tag. Hell, even the shooting feels satisfying and fun! And thats coming from someone who RARELY plays shooters. But that polish starts to fall away when the gameplay begins to feel stale, using the exact same loadout for the first few hours with no change, praying that whatever you unlock next is something you'll actually enjoy using.

Theres a real gem of a game here, it's just buried under layers of unfortunate, un-fun decisions, and quite a few timers.

Edit:: Since it was pointed out, it's worth saying that I actually played a handful of hours at a friends house before playing my own copy, so I have netted around 3 or so hours of gameplay. Take that how you will!

Before I say anything, I want it to be known that I desperately want this game to be as awesome as it looks on the surface. I just cannot recommend it at full price at the moment because of the following issues I have with it:

- There is no way to increase/upgrade the base damage your guns do. For a game like this to not offer some way to upgrade the damage you deal feels wrong, especially when you consider how violent the damage falloff is. It feels like every time I cross into mid-range combat damage falls from the mid 40s-50s to sub 20, even dropping to 1 in many cases (I'm talking about headshot/critical damage btw). There are also no melee weapons in the game currently, and the melee you do have has a cooldown so long it's essentially worthless against more than one enemy in close range.

- The counter for the Chaos mechanic has an rng chance to increase on ALL incoming damage. You are being actively punished for taking damage in this fps-soulslike-roguelike. I understand, and admittedly do enjoy the idea of the chaos mechanic, but if you want to punish the player for taking damage, I would recommend it be from damage that's caused by the TRAPS that trigger it, since that's readily avoidable damage, and not a projectile that can curve around corners or cross the map in a second. Alternatively, you could've had it be a time-based mechanic, where the longer you're in a level without entering the boss arena (say, maybe every 3-5 minutes or so), the higher the counter gets. It's not an egregious issue, since you CAN deal with and overcome the chaos events. But, more likely than not you'll be low on healing around the time it occurs, since the counter increases from damage you take and you carry like no healing items, and you'll be low on ammo and out of healing by the time you deal with it and decide "I don't want to lose the witchfire I've gathered. I want to level up," so you'll leave the level or die trying.

- The Gnosis upgrade mechanic (I have the most to say about this one). Gnosis is something that you are REQUIRED to upgrade to unlock the bosses of the game. The issue is that in deciding "I want to try and fight the boss of the level" you have now told the game to start arbitrarily spawning stronger, tankier mobs in the level you've been grinding on these past few hours, so now you need to grind for even MORE time because it seems like the elite mobs spawn in packs, are tanky as shit, and you still have to avoid ALL damage lest you incur the wrath of the chaos mechanic. That shouldn't be something the player's forced to deal with AFTER playing a level for multiple hours to prepare for the boss fight. Imagine if a Souls game did this. You really want to beat that first boss, so you keep grinding souls and leveling up, and then you level up your Gnosis to access the boss room, because it's MANDATORY, and now the game decides that since you've decided you're ready to face the boss, you get to deal with groups of elite/miniboss mobs that were NEVER spawning before that are multiple times tankier and spankier than the enemies you've been facing to this point, all while there's no way to increase the amount of damage your weapons deal. On top of that, you'll HAVE to deal with them if you want to fill out your perk tree for that run to stand a chance against the boss. Now don't get me wrong, I'm not saying the experience shouldn't be punishing or difficult, I do enjoy the Souls series after all. What I AM saying is that if you want elite/miniboss mobs to be in your levels, do as Souls does and simply have them spawn regardless of the player's level/gnosis level and they'll deal with them naturally as they improve, and not as an unexpected surprise when they finally engage with Gnosis only to find that the level they were just having a blast with has become the beaches of Normandy and they are NOT the one with the MG42. That'll turn more players away than it'll retain. OR in the earlier levels you could have these stronger enemies spawning in the hidden areas that you need a higher Gnosis level to unlock, that way the players encounter them organically and it's a fun challenge rather than a kick in the dick for wanting to enter the boss arena.

I'm hoping that some of the difficulty the game has right now is just there to pad for content, as it is early access and there isn't much to really do in the game right now. Beyond that, the levels are fun to play through, the spells and weapon abilities are fun, and if the difficulty didn't spike as hard as it did for simply wanting to unlock the boss arena I'd be singing a very different tune about this game. I'm not giving up on it, and I'll update my review if any of the things I've talked about here change, but right now I'd say give it some more time to cook and see where it goes or get it on sale.

This one’s got serious style — great visuals, crunchy gunplay, and a haunting world that oozes atmosphere. It feels like it should be something special. But after a few hours, you start to notice a problem: there’s nothing really in that beautiful world. No NPCs to talk to, no voices, no real story delivery, not even ambient murmurs to sell the setting. Just you, some demons, and the oppressive silence.
Combat is fun, sure. But it leans way too hard into the “you’re a one-man army” thing. That can work — if the world reacts to you or gives you context. Here, though, it just feels like you’re being thrown into an empty arena over and over again. The lack of co-op is baffling. The entire game loop practically begs for a buddy: exploring, fighting, failing together. But instead? You’re on your own — and not in a cool, survival-horror kind of way, more like “nobody showed up to the LAN party” kind of way.
The tutorial? Might as well not exist. It tells you almost nothing and just assumes you’ll figure it all out through sheer willpower or trial-and-error. Great for hardcore purists, terrible for anyone who values their time.
⸻
What needs to happen:
    •    Add NPCs, VO, or any world-building that isn’t a collectible or text box.
    •    Seriously rework the tutorial — make it intuitive, not cryptic.
    •    Strongly consider co-op. Even a simple drop-in/drop-out 2-player mode would completely change the vibe in a good way.
    •    The world is too pretty to be this empty. Fill it with something to care about.
⸻
TL;DR: Witchfire has a killer core — it looks and plays great — but right now it feels like a flashy demo with no soul. Bring in some characters, some story, some damn voices, and let us team up. If the devs can nail that, this could become a top-tier experience.

P.S. I will re-review it after full version of the game.

Witchfire is basically everything I was looking for in a PvE shooter, and I spent a long time looking for a halfway decent one that wasn't mind-numbingly boring.

Let's just get the bad part out of the way, because quite frankly there is a lot of good here. The worst part about this game *so far* is that there is only 2 maps available. Granted they do have a wide variety of weapons, spells, and more planned, I find that it does not deserve the current price tag of $40USD. Yes, the game is in early access and yes, not a lot of content is available at such an early stage. However, in my honest opinion, the game is not worth $40USD, more like $20-$25USD in its current state. That being said, this has to be one of the most "polished" early-access games that I have played.

Now that my one downside has been shared, let me tell you about all the other good things about this game. Firstly, the performance is spectacular. I've maybe had one or two times where my framerate drops, and that's due to a lot of particle effects being triggered upon entering certain areas. The graphics look amazing and I can easily run this game at 4k 120+FPS with my PC (YMMV as I have a 4090 and beefy PC specs.)

Second, the gameplay is amazing. The gunplay is S+ tier and it feels amazing to use any of the weapons and spells in the game. My only nitpick is that the damage falloff for each weapon is very sudden and with some experimenting you will eventually figure out what ranges your weapons work best in. The main problem with the damage falloff is if you take 1 step outside of the optimum/maximum range for the weapon, you will only deal 1 damage. Yes, 1 singular damage even if you headshot with a charged weapon. If they made the damage falloff scale with distance past the max weapon range, that would fix it.

Movement is super fluid and reminds me heavily of DOOM Eternal's physics. You move at a solid pace, sprinting is nice to have while traversing the map and for use in combat. You also get a nice double jump and a dash that is very snappy. Only thing is you can't dash in the air which is understandable but I still wish you could. If you wanted to be a DOOM slayer cosplaying as a witchunter, this game is that and more. It does have a stamina meter but I've barely leveled it and it has never been a problem.

The gameplay loop is pretty solid although a bit limited given that it is EA. That being said they absolutely nailed the core loop. Prep for combat by burning incense which is a one-time buff per expedition, and the resources to make them can be found easily while playing. Once you're on an expedition you have one of two goals you can set for yourself: grind the map for witchfire and other resources to level up and buff your character, or focus on completing the main quest of the map and any side quests you have set for yourself as well. Once you're ready to extract just make your way to a portal and clear it of enemies and wait for it to open. It also has a nod to souls-like games where if you die you lose all your resources, but you can return to the map in your next run and pick up everything you lost which is very nice.

Enemy variety is lacking a little bit, and it does feel like some of them are slightly overtuned (the arquebus/musketeers and the teleporting swordsman come to mind) but it's really only a problem if you get caught off guard or are facing off against 6+ at a time. Feels like the game is begging for a wave defense/arena combat scenario similar to that of classic COD zombies of spawning into an arena, kill enemies to gain currency, spend said currency to expand the map, get new weapons, level up some stats, and build defenses. It also *really* needs a coop mode, as I can see myself and some friends spending a lot of time playing this game.

For what little story there is, it is very servicable. The theming is on point and nothing about this game or its story elements feels out of place. There are little bits of lore dropped here and there in various scrolls you will find throughout the game, but it would be nice if we got just a little bit more.

Overall, I give this game an 8.5/10. However given that the game is in EA and has very little content available I would have to dock it down to a 6/10. What is here is very good and is worth playing if you get the game on a discount or for free through getting it gifted by a friend, but I would avoid shelling out the full $40USD until they at least have half the planned content available. That being said, the devs are cooking up something wonderful here and I am excited for future updates and added content. Until then I would give this game a pass for now, but do wishlist it and check in every so often

Was interested in this game as a soulslike but the gameplay just never clicked for me and felt very stale.

TLDR; I do not recommend it, but only barely. Game is slow and rewards a methodical play-style, and I'm hesitant to continue because of how the devs prioritize gun-play over spells, in addition to boring rogue-like boons that don't affect game-play much throughout each expedition. Each run feels almost the same. 

A pretty decent rogue-like extraction shooter combo, it has a lot of gun-play inspired aspects from Destiny (that is a good thing) like weapon frames. They do, however, also use a lot of "rogue-like" boons similar to destiny (that is a bad thing).

A lot of boons you earn throughout a play-through are pretty mild, and don't affect game-play all that much (including a whole whopping 1% extra drop rate for healing elixirs, wow), which makes each run feel nearly identical. Similarly, there is an emphasis on gun-play compared with the spells we earn and use, which I'm not a huge fan of. 

The spells feel pretty weak, and seem to be secondary to guns (even though ammo is also sparse), as they have pretty large cooldowns and very low damage. None of the heavy spells I've gotten so far are very satisfying or useful, especially for how long they take to recharge, and very few light spells are very useful either. Mostly they seem to be used for staggering enemies, or afflicting them with an elemental affix, which isn't bad in and of itself, but if that's their main purpose, their CDs should definitely be reduced imo. If their damage is so low, I don't understand why their cooldown isn't lower either. I'm sure it has to do with the balance they want with how fast-paced the game feels, since it definitely feels like a conscious decision, I just don't think it's a very good one.

Speaking of pace, the game is pretty slow. I saw someone else mention how it's a very dad-game, if that makes sense, and I can understand that view. It's not a bad thing, but man oh man I wish the game was faster. Even just a little, but more than a little would be better. I really really wish stamina consumption was not a thing out of combat, and everything generally feels very slow/sluggish once you get used to the dance of things. I'm not going to speak on the balance of weapons, but some certainly feel stronger than others. 

Ammo consumption is directly linked to how good at the stun mechanics you are, which is a great idea in concept, but feels kind of bad when you realize you're going to be doing 1/2 damage and losing ammo unless you're constantly abusing the stun mechanics, even when it doesn't feel necessary.

I'm not sure how often the devs update the game, although it's been one or two months since last I played and everything has been the same since then, and it's difficult to want to continue just because of how unbalanced the game feels with guns vs. spells. Maybe the later game is different, I don't know, but 7 hrs in and it isn't looking like it, even after unlocking the other inventory slots.

Falling off a cliff into void/depths also immediately ends your run, which generally I wouldn't mind, if it was my own fault. However usually, the circumstances are questionable. More often am I pushed horizontally by a projectile coming at me from a perpendicular angle than running off of my own volition. Projectiles *pulling* me forward and thus into an abyss is also an issue I have, especially when they look identical to all other projectiles and just behave differently for some reason. Or at least I assume they look identical, maybe they don't, but I've never noticed a difference.- look, I don't mind losing player autonomy, especially when it's purposeful, however when it happens for some willy-nilly, not-so-easily-identifiable reason, over and over again, it really knocks the wind out of your sails. Especially when that reason ends a long winded run unceremoniously. I'm not saying to remove the mechanic, but at least give only a specific enemy enemy the ability, or maybe give the projectile a very obvious look about it compared to the other projectiles. Something that allows players to know when there's a different threat to be aware of. Readability in games is a legitimate issue and one that isn't always obvious. This game has major fundamental issues that result in a very poor experience.

TL;DR, the game tries to be a lot of games at once without really having an identity of its own. The result of this identity crisis is a game that feels slow, over complicated, and unrewarding. These are not Early Access issues, but instead core mechanics and design decisions that will almost certainly be carried on to full release.

The good:

1. The idea of the game is exactly as cool as it sounds. It's a dark fantasy FPS where you hunt down zombies and demons using magic and cool weapons. It does nail the atmosphere to a degree, especially in the latter maps and the weapon designs. This is pretty much what makes people be interested in the game in the first place, and the main selling point as you can see from the trailers and highlights. Notice how you get very short cuts of the fights in the videos above. This is meant to show the overall vibe of the game rather than prolonged pieces of gameplay.

The bad:

1. The gameplay loop is EXTREMELY repetitive and short of content. You basically spawn in a map, clear about 6 camps containing the same enemies in slightly different combinations, do that one puzzle, maybe kill that one boss, get the same 3 or 4 items and return. The thing you do on your first hour is the same thing you will be doing 6 hours later, no changes, no variation. You'd think this is the definition of a rouguelike, but the issue is there's virtually NO VARIATION between runs. Your build won't change from one run to the other. The changes are so minimal and so spread out that a vast majority of runs end up feeling the same way. If you want to get a new weapon / spell / item you have to complete a lot of runs to get the currency to then complete more runs to finish the research, to finally equip that ONE new item.

2. The maps. This game's level design is very bad. And I don't mean the atmosphere of course. I mean the actual design of the level. The layouts are bland, flat and empty. The first map is basically an island in the most basic sense of the word. It has a few trees, a few paths, and that's pretty much it. Then you unlock the second map, hoping it will be better, and it's so incredibly similar you think you selected the wrong map accidentally. The same coast, the same trees, the same paths. This is jarring because the few zones that take you indoors into dark corridors and castles are by far the best, but they're a minority. The levels feel like they're amateurishly crafted maps with a dark fantasy coat of paint. Once you get past the awe of the atmosphere, they feel uninspired and uninteresting. Not to mention that the maps play absolutely no role in the gameplay. No use of architecture or level design to make fights interesting or engaging. Enemies will spawn in random pieces of barren land and start swinging. The camps you're clearing? just a bunch of enemies that spawn in a spot, don't expect an actual camp or a building or anything.

The worst:

1. The progression system. The worst design decision that could have been made by far is the inclusion of this game's soulslike system. Get "souls", spend a million souls to upgrade a stat by an unnoticeable point, rinse and repeat. It makes progression feel completely unrewarding and pointless. The difference between vitality level 1 and level 2 is a tiny percentage of health. This makes your permanent upgrades and progress feel like a drop in a tall glass of boredom. If you compound this with the fact that there are only a handful of perks to pick inside the expeditions themselves, the result is an extremely slow and repetitive gameplay loop.

Summarizing, I wish this game had put more thought behind the gameplay loop and level design to make it an experience that remains fun after more than a couple of hours.

In Witchfire's current state, I'm leaning towards not recommending.

The reasons are below:
- $39.99 is too high for a game that's missing a lot of content. At least half of the levels are not available, skills are not available, lack of weapon variety, no core game mechanic explanations, and wonky gameplay. Yes, I know the game is still in Early Access, but I think $24.99 would be a better price in it's current state.

- Starting classes overlap too much or don't have much differences besides point allocations and starting weapons. I think it's a better idea to set a starting level at 10 (or whatever) and allow the user to allocate points as they see fit. At the end of the day, the only difference in the classes is how they look.

- Bad weapon damage and running out of ammo far too frequently. There doesn't seem to be any significant damage increase from "surprise" attacks or headshots. This in turn makes some weapons redundant or not useful because why would I use a slower firing rifle when I can spam the revolver (which also does more damage)? Additionally, damage drop-off is huge. In other words, the farther you are from an enemy, the less damage you do. You'll commonly see 1 damage at medium distance. I understand this is done so you, as the player, can't just snipe your way to victory, but it highlights an issue with ranged weapons like rifles...what's the point of using ranged weapons when you're heavily penalized, damage-wise, for ranged combat? Another example is the shotgun. It shows a base damage of 80 but at pointblank range, I've seen damage in the low 40s.

- You can only jump twice before stamina runs out. Stamina runs out sliding about 3 times. This really needs to be adjusted because stamina drains far too quickly when jumping or sliding.

- Some enemy projectiles track far too well. This wouldn't be a problem if you had an ability to avoid enemy projectiles. You do have a sliding ability, but you have to be in a sprint and move somewhat sideways/diagonal. You can sprint sideways, but when there's a lot of enemies, it because cumbersome. I think an easy fix would decrease how well enemy projectiles turn and track.

- No explanations for core mechanics such as leveling, increasing skills, increasing weapon abilities, etc. There is a tutorial that explains how combat mechanics work, but there's nothing regarding core mechanics. I figured out things as I played, but it would help to explain things. It would especially be helpful regarding status effects. I was at the "secret" area of the first map where you have to kill all the cave guardians in certain time limit. You get to a part where there's a "Sanity" status effect. I have no idea how I got this status effect and died after the "Sanity" meter depleted multiple times. It became frustrating because there's zero explanations of where it came from, what it does, and how to avoid it. I died multiple times in this area because of this.

- I really dislike games where enemies scale with you. It makes "leveling up" redundant and very un-rewarding. I hope a better way to implement difficulty is done to avoid enemy scaling.

- Reloading for the bolt action rifles needs to be fixed when it's a partial reload. When there's at least one bullet in the bolt action rifle and you reload, the animation is shown to cycle the bolt after a new magazine is inserted. This is not necessary because the rifle is already loaded with an un-fired bullet. Cycling the bolt on a partial reload would actually eject the un-fired bullet from the rifle.

- Game has crashed a few times, and occasionally, I get really bad frame drops. I am running at 4k at max settings with a 4090. Witchfire could use better optimization.

TLDR: Witchfire has potential, but in it's current state, I'd pass. Priced too high for being Early Access with the amount of content provided and lack of core game mechanics being explained. Most issues stem from the fact the game needs more time in development and testing to iron out gameplay issues as well. Unfortunately, Steam doesn't allow in the middle recommendations, which I would give this game. It needs a bit more polishing.

I'm sad because this game absolutely slaps prior to Gnosis 2. 

At which point the game takes the piss.  I don't mind brutal difficulty I have thousands of hours across the souls series and Armored Core. I enjoy damn hard.  What bothers me is how fast It snowballs into intentionally burning all of your resources because you made a mistake.  The Calamity Meter seems like a really cool idea, but in practice it becomes. "Not only do you lose resources, not only did we burn your pots, not only did you lose ammo and HP, you now have a fuck hard extra battle to drain you even more! Oh wait did you not kill it fast enough so a hunter is now on your ass? Well too bad guess  what meter is snowballing again! Oh you got grazed by an artillery shot, lemme ad an other pip onto the meter."

It is extremely easy if you are not playing absolutely perfect, or get caught by a stray you couldn't have seen coming, to cause that meter to add another ten minute gunfight onto your run. Were you going for a boss kill? Well you now don't have the resources you need to do that, because of how easy it is to just chain shenanigans. 

The player is already being punished when they get hit, that's the point behind a health bar. That's the point behind hard rooms.  Spending Ammo, Spending HP, and spending potions is the main draw of a souls level of difficulty. Tacking on the Calamity meter means that if you ever fuck up *too much* which in most sane games is death, you are taxed further. Even if you only trigger the calamity, and never get hit, your ammo stores are still shot to fuck and back during the battle. If you have enough ammo to limp through it you do get rewarded pretty heavily but not enough to ever stem the bleeding. 


The rewards do offset the calamity meter quite a lot, and I like that as an idea, but it in practice makes me dread doing any room harder than four dudes drunk on a beach because it wastes time. Even if the Calamity were strict upside if you were good, it's a giant time sink. 

It makes each run so much longer and not in an interesting way. It's just more dudes, more bullet sponging. 

Which is a shame because the overworl exploration, and risk reward systems prior to Gnosis 2 are fucking awesome.  I really enjoyed systematically dismantling the islands defenses and ripping through hordes of dudes. I felt powerful but frail. It was a really cool balance of 'yes your guns absolutely fuck but so do your enemies be careful'.  That goes away after Gnosis 2. The threat of the Calamity meter and the random hunters, and the constant boss enemies, are all very annoying and take me out of the vibes of the early game.  That wouldn't be enough for me to not recommend it though. 

The thing that kills this game for me is the borderless fullscreen performance is actually ass.  Fullscreen at the same resolution 1440p, ran easily 20% lighter.  (40% GPU usage fullscreen 60% borderless). 

I would get random dips in framerate, weird 1% lows, and hitching in borderless. Fullscreen? Runs like a champ. 

So just play it in fullscreen right?

Let me paint a picture for you. You're playing the shipwreck map and go to the shore to clear it out. Farther up the beach there is a cliff face with bowmen who spawn on the top of the cliff. You don't notice them at first because they're so far away that they don't even show up on your HUD. You are finally alerted to their presence by them knocking off a third of your health. You aim to take a shot, but then remember that even with your long range weapon it'll do little to no damage at this distance, and even if you did decide to chip away at their health you'd run out of ammo before you could kill them. So you decide to go to the top and face them directly. The path that takes you up there from the beach is an uphill slope that brings you directly into the range of some musketmen, swordsmen, and if you're unlucky even a miniboss musketman who is a damage sponge and deadeye even when you dash right before he fires. While you contend with these enemies to gain the cliff those bowmen come down the cliff to help them, turning your assault into a retreat with this mob hot on your heels.
You really only have two options now. The first is to stand your ground and fight. This is a terrible idea because of how many enemies you'd have to fight all at once, and even with the proper utilization of spells and dodging you'd likely run out of ammo before they're all dead. Not to mention that you get a limited amount of heals and the dropchance of ammo or healing vials are too slim to rely on most of the time. 
The second choice is to try and get the group separated and take them on piecemeal. This is also not a great choice because enemies don't seem to have an aggro limit or range to how far they follow. On the first map I aggro'd two enemies at the base of the tower and they followed me nearly to the spawning area at that beach until I realized they wouldn't stop following me. And remember when I said how their damage doesn't have damage falloff? Yeah that's still a problem.
TL;DR your options boil down to be washed away in a tide of enemies or be shot to pieces trying to run away.

This wouldn't be so bad if it wasn't for the damage falloff on certain weapons. I can see why it would be so dramatic on something like a shotgun or maybe your starter pistol. But at present it's just ridiculous and forces you into dangerous situations that you probably aren't equipped to handle this early on. That's the only big issue the game has right now as far as I can tell. Though I will say that I'm not a huge fan of the lack of initial customization you get when you pick your "class". It would be nice to be able to just make a custom preyer class. But I can see why they don't have it since it's most likely a balancing issue.

The review is negative right now but that's only because of the damage issue. I'll update it after it's addressed and I'll probably do a completely new review once the game is out of EA.

I've tried coming back to this a few times, hoping something will change since it's early access but every time I just end up sorely disappointed and uninstall the game. In blunt terms, it just feels like the devs don't know what in God's name they're doing. 

The game feels like it's got a serious identity crisis going on. On one hand, it feels like it wants to be a run and gun FPS with an emphasis on exploration. On the other hand, it also feels like it's trying to be like Dark Souls, where mobility is limited due to a stamina system, even the weakest enemies hit like a truck, and regaining health is limited to a very limited consumable. When you take combat encounters that are clearly designed to take a fast and loose approach in the vein of Painkiller or Serious Sam and then slap on a mobility system where you move fairly slow and have to rely on dodging which consumes stamina, then throw the fact that restoring health is limited to using healing elixrs, of which you can only carry a very small amount and are an extremely rare drop on the field, it just doesn't work. There's a reason why good run and gun shooters are usually generous with health items. 

Then there's the weapons. The weapons have a lot of potential. They've got some pretty cool designs and they're fun to shoot. The issue is their damage drop off is ludicrous. Having damage drop off outside a weapon's effective range is common and fine but the issue is that in Witchfire the rate at which damage drops off is just ridiculous.  If you're more than a couple inches outside your weapon's effective range, the damage your gun does instantly drops down to 1.

Then there's the sort of parry system it's got going on. Basically if you dodge while near an enemy a circle appears near them that you can shoot to stun them for a few seconds. It's pretty clear the devs want you to make heavy use of this but at the same time it's extremely finnicky. I've tried all sorts of things with it and the best I can figure it boils down to "it works when it feels like working".

At this point I'd say your best bet is to just skip out on this one. The game has been in Early Access for a while now and I really can't see the devs making any changes to address the issues with the game m

I also find the roguelike elements during the runs to be of low impact, really the gear you bring into the run is the most important. So far I haven't had any rune pickups that changed how the run was going to be played. I hope that future updates add some exciting powerups instead of the generic: more stamina, better healing, more witchfire drops, etc. Those are boring and are of low impact. The secrets offered by Gnosis I feel pretty underwhelming, its basically just more ammo chests and occasionally a door that will have an item that sells for some gold. I wish it was more impactful, considering how hard the game gets after you unlock it. 

Maybe I just botched my character though ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Witchfire is one of those games that you get when the devs are talented but directionless fans. Instead of something that's great and unique, Witchfire ends up playing like a list of the games that these developers love.
Souls/Remnant games, Apex, Hades perhaps, and a dash of extraction. While it's a great time killer, there's nothing to really draw you in and keep you playing. Just to list off a few fundamental issues that I have with the game:

Same maps on repeat. While this would be fine in a BR or extraction game due to other players providing the variable experience in matches, this is just a single player game. So it turns into a repetitive grind that only changes when you unlock gnocchi [sic] which opens up more of the maps with challenges, albeit very small extra areas. I feel like this just induces burnout more than anything in a single player game. 

Great Apex-like movement, no reason to use it. Seriously the long, fast slides feel very Apexy. Apex, as you might recall, is strictly PVP. I have no reason (or at least, haven't yet) to be taking these risky high-pace movements. I made great use of sliding in Apex, often grappling for momentum and flinging myself behind them to come out ahead. I am failing to see a reason to slide myself into a bunch of enemies that will stun lock that shit out of me.

The inventory/stash system???? What even is this? Why do unused keys go there and why can't I bring them with me?? I've got 30 useless keys in there. 

The level up system is just a mockery of a Souls game. Like it's maybe 12% endearing that you took inspiration from Fromsoft, but 88% embarrassing and kind of insulting that this is how you chose to show it. There is one single offensive stat that reduces spell cool down. Two supporting/ancillary stats to make the game a bit easier (one gives more souls, one increases item spawn) and then you have vigor, endurance, and a "heal more from your potions" stat. So what is the build here? Either vigor or endurance dump, or maybe cast spells a bit more often. No damage, no real variation, and therefore no purpose or reason to care about it. 

It does look pretty good though, animations are nice, guns are detailed, environment is fairly pretty and gives kind of an open world feel which is necessary, especially considering it's a hub-based game. But as long as it remains a mish mash of influences it will only be maybe a 5/10 game for me. I can see how some people enjoy it, but I truly believe most of these positive reviews will actually burn out within 10 hours of game play and change their minds.
