This whole review is based about the fact that this game is advertised as a rouguelite: it isn't.

Almost nothing that matters changes between runs (with the same Gnosis). 
The enemies are the same. The mini quests are the same. The arcana you get are the same. 
The only major thing that changes is just the position of the encounters, but the underlying map stays the same.

The stats you get by leveling up are also a bit disapponting, there's basically only defensive stats (HP regen by consuming potions, dash speed), the only offensive stat just reduces magic cooldown.
This hurts the RPG part of the game a lot (why can't I, as a mage, put tons of level up in magic dmg disregarding defenses? Why can't another class, I don't know, have low magic damage but high pistol damage, or low hp but tremendous damage? et similia.)
There's no build variety, every class ends up feeling the same and having the same stats even in the early game.

Granted, some of those things are probably because it's EA, but if you take roguelites/likes such as TBOI and Hades, you can clearly see the difference about what a rouglelite is meant to be.

This game is just frustrating. It starts nice and fun, but at some point the difficulty skyrockets. You have no tools to deal with enemies that can shoot you from 5 miles away hidden behind tree textures so you can't even see them, you constantly get stuck in small rocks on the road while trying to side roll the enemy attacks, then there's grenadier, he can snipe you with a sequence of AOE mortar attacks and it doesn't matter where you are. If you get hit, you lose focus, but without focus you can't deal with harder enemies because they can simply bulldoze you. You can stun them if you roll and hit their weak spot, but only if you have focus. So in a high level fight one mistake usually means you have to retreat and quite likely die. It's hard to hit enemies because the animations are jerky. The progression feels slow. The orb collection quest is ridiculously slow. The areas that open in earlier levels as you progress don't feel rewarding and are just unnecessary. The gear like rings and amulets are so weak, more often than not they hinder instead of helping, like the ring that creates explosions when you roll, guess what: they do negative damage but you can't see sh*t because of their VFX.

Good things: guns collection is wide and interesting to explore, although some guns feel superior. Shooting feels satisfying when the animations and AI work properly and don't jitter.

Meh things: music in the menu is super cool but in the gameplay it's repetitive and nothing special. Level design is quite boring and you'll have to backtrack a lot. Some parts of the game look beautiful, but overall it felt like just another level in the forest/with rocks/with broken boats.

I understand that the game is in early access and many things may change before the release. But for now I can't recommend it.

The Prayer Bead system just sucks, two isn't enough pre-gnosis 2, four isn't enough at three/four when there's seemingly more than 40 plus and they all have effects you'd see in a perk tree in any other roguelike and can be reliably grinded at any stage of the game. Stats are here because.... dev really wants you to put all your points into flesh and mind so that you can survive exactly ONE hit from a boss or melee unit and heal back up, or get threetapped by anything, and munitions exists so you have to put points into it to do anything at *actual* range (why are bolt-actions doing crap damage at range? Don't farm on lower levels, powergrind to higher gnosis and you'll waste less time grinding on lower tiers because higher tiers literally give double to triple what you get on lower tiers. You're welcome.

Leveling up will not only require an ever increasing amount of witchfire (souls), which is pretty par for the course in games like these but the difficulty is tied directly to your level. The devs have tried to set the record straight on this, saying it doesn't, but what they mean is enemy health isn't tied to your level, but other things get harder. There will be more enemies and existing enemies now having shields, effectively giving them more health, and now that enemy is shooting at you, and then suddenly there will be more powerful enemies etc etc ... effectively meaning the game is harder despite the devs denials. Whilst leveling up only gives you a miniscule 2% improvement per level, it won't make you more powerful because every level you upgrade results in the game cranking up the difficulty, so you're not actually getting stronger comparatively. And the jump in required witchfire is sometimes excessive. Once it jumped from 28K to over 40k the next time.  

The game will turn deadly within a few levels and upgrading to meet the challenge will only make the game harder each time you do it, but not just a little bit, and is akin to shooting yourself in the foot because you're only making your life harder by doing it, except you have to do it fully unlock upgrades for weapons. 

Regarding that, there are a whole host of long range, medium range and short range weapons. None of these weapons can be found in the wild, they all have to be researched and upgraded by researching (which really just means using them) and then using gold which is bought with increasing amounts of witchfire. There's also light spells and heavy spells, not forgetting rings, fetishes and Relics to be unlocked by being researched and then by farming ever increasing amounts of witchfire, and upgraded individually by using them in the game. This means that individual spells take an eternity to upgrade because you will only be able to kill a few enemies every run with them and in total you will have to kill about 400 enemies to fully upgrade some spells.  So, how many times do I have to go out and kill enemies at about 10, 15 minutes a time, to upgrade a single spell to max level? A LOT!

To make a long story short, the amount of grinding, farming of enemies to upgrade gear and get witchfire, to get the required gold to unlock all these weapons, spells etc etc as well as the individual upgrades for each  as well as upgrading my character in general, makes my level 400 Elden Ring character look cheap in comparison. Oh you can upgrade your ability to acquire witchfire so you can upgrade faster, but it's a measly 2% at a time, but guess what, the game will crank up the difficulty every time you do it, so in reality you will make yourself comparatively weaker, and your gains getting witchfire will be marginal at best. It's bonkers!

Regarding health, at level 20 you will only have a maximum 3 health potions, 4 and level 35 and then max level is only 5 at level 50, which fill my health by about half each time and the worst part is that's only as long as I farmed a plant called Angelica while I'm out and about or won't have any health potions at all. I think farming health is a no no! Especially because you can only pick up a few plants a run if you're lucky. Have you never heard of refillable estus flasks? 

A game shouldn't be this much hard work!

Also, there are areas called vaults which are not only difficult but on a timer putting you under enormous pressure to do them fast when slow and steady should win the race. Remove the damn timer for the love of you know what!  There also calamities which flood enemies into area and make your life a nightmare! 

Each map has portals and you will get sent to random one each time, which means you probably won't get the one you want which gives you no alternative other than leave and try again, and again, and again, over and over!  When you want to get to the boss and you can't get the nearest portal, it's beyond annoying. Just let me choose the portal I want. 

I've been doing the Galley Slave boss fight. Firstly, the portal is miles away from the boss. Even if you can get near the boss fight without having to battle through hordes to get to the actual boss gate there will be enemies directly outside who will see you regardless, even if you're not in their line of sight and will have to deal with them before you go in because the boss arena is completely open to any enemies outside.  Nearly every time I've done the fight there's a calamity and other enemies flood the boss arena.  I really think this needs to be thought through.  If the boss deliberately spawned his own minions, that's one thing but dealing with enemies running into the boss arena from outside is another thing entirely.

In that regards, calamities in general are beyond annoying. When I want to do a boss, calamity. Doing a vault, calamity. Just doing a bit of farming, calamity. You can guarantee, almost every time you venture out there will be a calamity. I understand the reasoning behind it as it really adds an element of unpredictability but they're far too easy to set off and this is the thing that mostly made me stop playing.

I absolutely love this game, but it has a lot of problems in its current state. The biggest being the difficulty and progression. There is a lot of RNG going on behind the scenes determining what the run will be, however it comes in one or two flavors, tediously easy, or outright unfair as hordes spawn on your location, curses rain down on you spawning endless enemies, with you armed with weapons that simply are not powerful enough, or with ammo reserves not deep enough to handle the sheer numbers getting thrown at you. The further and further I get into the game, the more and more I am succumbing to unfair deaths. The stamina system does more to leave you hobbled, rather than act as a crucial resource to manage, as when in combat, keeping tabs on a thin line, at the out most edge of the screen isn't viable, when you have to actively time dodges as not to get hit from every conceivable angle. With most enemies having ranged attacks and being surrounded being the norm, use of cover often isn't possible, leaving you to dash to dodge incoming attacks, leaving you slow, and absurdly vulnerable when your stamina inevitably depletes. Spells are largely useless with how ridiculously long they take to recharge, you either have to save them for something big, or just get used to not having them. The progression system feels meaningless, as each level, your upgrade is so minuscule, that it takes a dozen or so levels specked into a single stat to have any tangible impact on gameplay. With most equipment progression gated, you are woefully under equipped to actually progress through the game, leaving you to grind out the same couple of levels for basic resources to level up, which become exponentially more expensive each level, meaning even more grinding. There may be a far more optimal gameplay loop than what I have found myself in, but the game does little to guide you outside the most utterly basic information, leaving you to grope about for meaning behind everything getting thrown at you. Again, I love this game, but it doesn't do much well, and poor design choices bog down what should be a stellar experience into frustrating tedium.

Pros
The combat feels excellent, with highly satisfying visuals, impactful camera work, and impressive bullet effects.
The game environment is stunning, making exploration enjoyable.
The Gacha equipment system adds an exciting layer of progression.
Each weapon has unique effects, creating diverse and interesting gameplay styles.
I appreciate mechanics that punish mistakes, like the calamity bar increasing when taking risks or making errors—it adds an extra layer of challenge.
Overall, the game is solid, and I plan to keep playing.
Cons
The price feels too steep for the amount of content available. After 15 hours, I’ve completed all three levels and earned 17 out of 20 achievements. The game needs significantly more content to justify its cost.
The stamina system is overly punishing. Losing large amounts of stamina when hit makes later levels frustrating since you get hit frequently. Stamina is required for everything except walking, so escaping enemies becomes nearly impossible once you run out. You're left with two options: "spray and pray" or slowly walk away, hoping to survive. Worse, shooting and jumping prevent stamina regeneration, making the system feel overly restrictive. This is easily my least favourite mechanic in the game—it creates a frustrating loop that feels unfair rather than challenging.
While the visuals are excellent, they have a very distinct UE5 look. This isn’t necessarily bad, but as more games adopt this style, it starts feeling less unique. I prefer a more distinctive art direction.
Conclusion
Right now, I can’t recommend the game, mainly due to its high price relative to the content. The gameplay loop is enjoyable, but with such limited content, it becomes repetitive quickly—at least for me. If the game receives more content in the future, I might reconsider, but as it stands, it doesn’t feel like it offers enough value for the cost.

Witchfire is a really good shooter mired in some weird and contradictory design decisions that make the gameplay more frustrating than enjoyable for me. When the game gets out of its own way, it feels awesome, with very snappy combat and fun powers. The atmosphere is great, and the performance is well optimized, with only occasional dropped frames in some environments. As far as the core gameplay is concerned, it should be a slam dunk.

But then the game gets too “clever” for its own good. Witchfire mixes elements of soulslikes, extraction shooters, roguelites, and traditional RPG leveling, but these elements clash in weird and tedious ways. The need to level up ends up gating you constantly, and it’s really the primary thing that matters in terms of how well you will do in a run (the roguelite in-run ability unlocks are underwhelming and don’t actually make for meaningfully different runs, at least at the levels I’ve reached so far), which makes the game loop come down to just repeating the same couple levels again and again with very little meaningful variation and playing in the most boring way possible to grind resources.

For example, you start the game with very little stamina. Stamina is what helps you dodge enemy attacks. This is important because on the first island, all of the enemies you encounter have attacks that target you without fail (some are slow heat-seeking missiles; others are fast deadeye shots, and others are melee attackers with teleport mechanics). So with your limited stamina, you can only dodge one or two of these attacks before you need to rest behind cover. But the game spawns enemies in groups of 4-6 right next to (often behind) you. If you encounter more than one swordsman at a time, you just die; you can’t run from them and can’t effectively fight them, because the game hasn’t given you tools to do so at the start. What you have to do is spend a while dipping into the level, shooting from cover, finding a bit of gold and witchfire, and leaving so you can level up and unlock more guns. This isn’t a tense experience, so it doesn’t work as an extraction shooter, really. Either you trigger the right mobs and it’s kind of too easy, or you trigger the wrong ones, and you get overwhelmed and die. It’s just kind of a rote experience you have to get through, so that you can level up enough to play the real game.

And you do, and the game starts to feel a bit fun. Then you meet the first boss. His attacks also home in on you, and they have very wide area of effects. So wide that your newly leveled up stamina isn’t leveled up enough for you to be able to dodge them with a single dodge. And every time he hits you, he takes out half your health bar and chunks down your stamina, which makes you less able to dodge. Basically, trying to beat him without leveling your stamina significantly is going to end up with you dying, and since you can only fight him after clearing the entire island, you end up clearing the whole island multiple times, just to lose all the resources in a boss fight that feels cheap and unfair. The smart play is the boring one again–farm some resources, then walk away, multiple times, until you’re leveled up enough.

Meanwhile, many of the game’s mechanics are cryptic and obtuse and can only really be understood via googling, so you often just get killed by things you can’t possibly understand (like a pirate ship that shows up mid bossfight for reasons and kills you by quickly draining a sanity meter you didn’t know you had).


Out of sheer obstinance, I powered through, I leveled up, and I became one of 20% of steam players to actually beat the first boss (that feels like a pretty low percentage to me, and indicative of how many people aren’t enjoying the experience of the early game enough to keep going–it’s the first boss, after all). It felt like I accomplished something, of a sort. And I was starting to learn enough of the game. Maybe it would be more fun-challenging and less punishing-hard now.

I leveled up my gnosis (difficulty) to unlock some more weapons, because item progression is hard-locked by your gnosis level. And one of my next tasks was to explore a crypt. And I’ll just say that the crypt is one of the most frustratingly artificially “hard” level designs I’ve ever encountered in a game. And I realized that it wasn’t a matter of getting past the first cheap boss to unlock the fun game. This is just how the game does difficulty; it wants to be a hard game so badly that it mistakes what makes a lot of hard games fun. I don’t feel challenged by tense encounters; I feel punished by obtuse rulesets, level gates, and odd mechanics. The shooting (because this is a shooter, in the end)--is actually maybe a bit easy, if anything.

I’m sure I’ll get some responses telling me to “git gud” and saying I’m playing the game the wrong way. I’ve seen plenty of such responses to other criticisms of this game, where folks say “It really clicks at about ~30 hours in.” And I know that for some people, Witchfire will be exactly what they want.

For me, it’s too tedious and frustrating in its current state to justify spending that kind of time on it. I don’t want to wait for a game to get enjoyable, googling obscure mechanics and hidden traps and cursing at hard level gates while I slog to level up and unlock the promise of what the game could be.

It’s still early access, so this all might change (I don’t suspect it will significantly, because a lot of the problems, really, are design choices, not implementation flaws, and it’s quite late in early access at this point). I’ll come back and reassess and update my review after it hits 1.0. But until then, I’m done trying to git gud and done waiting for the game to git gud too.

Edit: 
Y'all: my criticism is not that the game is hard (I like hard games): it's that the mechanics it uses to be "hard"  are just grindy roadblocks and cheap gotchas that make the game repetitive and not actually very skill-based.

On its surface, Witchfire promises the combat loop of a Destiny or Doom: an aggressive, movement-heavy shooter where you experiment with loadouts and abilities on the fly and where the challenge comes from adapting to a wide variety of enemy attack patterns. And maybe it becomes that…eventually.

But it starts you with no mobility, no equipment, long cooldowns, and next to no health until you grind through a bunch of levels. It rewards you for playing in a risk-averse way (extracting early is always more rewarding than pushing your luck and losing everything, and getting hit is punishing in unrecoverable ways). So the actual way you play the game for the first 10 hours is to farm the same five mobs on the same 2 levels from a safe difference and extract as soon as things get risky.

If the devs removed the grindy leveling, the extraction-shooter rewards, the insanity mechanic, and the slow-drip level-gated unlock of loot from this game…it might be a lot of fun. But while those things are in there, it's not worth slogging through 10+ hours of a bad game to hopefully unlock a good one.

- Weapon balance is all over the place, some guns are amazing, others useless.

- Enemies deal too much damage, with too many insta-kill mechanics. Even with full HP investment it feels like you still die in 3 hits instead of 2 hits.

- Enemy difficulty is inconsistent, some are pushovers, others absurdly strong.

- Maps feel extremly repetitive.

- Roguelite mechanics are weak. Most buffs are random and borderline useless. If I had to choose between +10% dmg/+10% HP or all other upgrades combined, I’d still pick the first.

- Some mechanics (like the Vestal Flame), feel meaningless.

- The rewards for the map events are laughable.

- Ammo... holy shit, I actually like the idea of weapon switching and looking for new ammo, but later maps are just stupid. Enemies turn into sponges that eat all your bullets, and even if you skill mostly for extra ammo, there’s still way too little.

The good:

- Itemization is fun,  there are many items for different playstyles.

- Weapons and gunplay feel great, even if the balance needs work.

- Graphics are solid, and the art style is at times exceptionally beautiful and haunting.

Conclusion:
There’s a good foundation here, but the balance, progression, and roguelite elements really need improvement. Not worth 40 Euro..

I have edited this review a couple of times trying to explain how the game has various issues with enemy attack hitboxes or gamefeel where your weapons don't actually get to do more damage they just get things like "Aim at 3 enemies to lock onto them and your bullets will bounce between them for 50% damage and proc a lighting bolt between them every 7 bounces."

The progression doesn't actually make YOU do more damage scaling up. Like you don't slowly get bigger and bigger numbers and there very much is a plateau where you have a damage cap which you have to try and circumvent to mediate enemy spawn clutter in the third (Currently final) map which causes most people once they hit Gnosis 3 to have horrible ammunition and suitability issues.

Gnosis is akin to "Bonfire Asceitic" from DS2. If you know...You know. Enemies get more prevalent and the higher HP and more irritating enemies spawn more frequently. As the dev says "Their HP remains the same no matter the Gnosis." which is true except for Elite enemies which spawn more at higher Gnosis. 


1. You can get more health, potions/estus, stamina to dodge but your guns themselves don't ever get more damage they just get gimmicky "Hold aim and fire at final moment for bonus damage" or "Lock onto 3 enemies and have bullets bounce at 50% damage with an arc of lightning between them every 7 bounces." but the weapons themselves will from start to finish not actually grow in their flat damage.

2. Ammo is a major issue at higher difficulties/Gnosis on the current final map. 

Explanation: 
The enemies are more clustered and the ammo boxes you find spread around said cluster poorly. Meaning if you had a particularly difficult situation where in your attempt to be mobile and avoid getting swarmed you ended up backing into another group, and another group, and ended up with a "Horde issue" and can very easily run out of ammo before you make it to an actual ammo box. There are purchasable consumable ammo pouches but those are limited you can hold per run and don't fully fill your ammo.

3. You become reliant on gimmick combos of weapons and spells later on. While this seems like a continuation of #1 this one is about "Fun" so understand that that joyful feeling of "I HAVE FINISHED FARMING AND I AM HERE TO CLEAR" you can get with RPG's is completely absent. This can limit your enjoyment pretty severely.

4. Stamina for sprinting and dodge are tied but you lose stamina from being hit, using a certain sniper rifle, and dodging repeatedly VERY QUICKLY. This makes you move slower, easier to get chain-hit, and unable to dodge until you have enough stamina to fill one dodge. This making the situation scale far worse against you depending on being swarmed.

5. Enemy melee hitboxes are wack and have about 6 more feet to hit than they should. Their bullets and spells are on point but melee is awful.

6. Snipers are useless. There is a chargable basic rfifle that can out-damage snipers and has near 2.5 times the ammo when you max it. There is also a sniper which to use causes your stamina to drain aka your dodge which is a terrible idea when to aim you usually want to be still for a moment which can already be impossible if swarmed. All in all from difficulty finding windows to scope in to their terrible ammo pool and mediocre gimmicks for upgrades they get binned pretty quickly.

7. Spells don't feel good. They do not have damage themselves and you can't go around being a wizard with a gun as secondary if you now what I mean. The spells work as stuns or debuffs or even a sort of "Totem" radiating damage if you follow it's mechanic but you don't ever just throw a big ass fireball and kill a group of enemies or call down a thunderstorm to cover an area. They feel truly secondary to guns and if you were wanting that spells OR guns then this game is very much not for you.

8. Game poorly explains it's own mechanics (Beyond weapons/trinkets/spells) and a lot is in text when to the gameplay junky can get skipped in thinking they will look at it later...Which if you skip because you just want more gameplay can end up with you upgrading Gnosis too early and making the game far less fun for you by upping it's difficulty (More spawns, less ammo, difficulty unique enemies and elites) before you finish upgrading weapons, spells, and trinkets before tackling them.

9. Upgrades/Boons for clearling a skull AKA a cluster of enemies feel insignificant outside of 3 which are reload speed, firing speed for not automatic fire, and what amounts to a "Glass cannon" perk.

10. The "GTA STARS" mechanic built into the game which can occur while fighting for your life can easily overwhelm you in the third map requiring you to use an item to reduce it which defeats the point of it really being there once you have it and makes it incredibly frustrating to deal with..Tiresome specifically, and should you forget and not have a way out means that the run can be essentially over as you can be low on ammo, health, or potions and have no way out to deal with what that event spawns and attacks you with.

11. Ultimately there isn't much here. For a roguelike the growth is limited and again with damage growth essentially capped you can never overtake the game and "Bully the bullies" like you can with roguelikes in general. You end up seeing the same enemies after a while and with the same 2 weapons, 2 spells, and 2 trinkets you end up growing bored.

12. Early access is not an excuse for dull or frustrating gameplay. Community currently is trying to jingle that in front of you like a pair of keys to a toddler to distract your from an otherwise dull game when you finish upgrading gear.

This game is a very mixed bag. It has bugs that were acknowledged by the devs 4 months ago, 3 maps, and some of the worst bosses that a video game can have...but it's still so, so much fun. The game is also gorgeous, and once you find the weapon that appeals to you, the gameplay loop is just addictive. I have "Beaten" all the content in the game for the moment, but I still have an itch to play more. It's just fun. Flawed in so many ways, but fun. 

I'll start with quick points for the bad and good features at a glance, then go into detail afterwards. I like getting the bad out of the way first. 

The Bad:
-Difficulty is forced and artificial. Half of the mechanics in the game are designed 'poorly' just to be harder rather than more fun. Bosses are worse than things I've seen from 5$ indie games. Dodging is a cursed tool for myriad reasons, but largely because the geometry will leave you constantly stuck on the smallest of debris. The vast majority of the damage I take in this game is from dodging and getting stuck on something that I previously walked over with no trouble. 

-Buggy. Devs will acknowledge bugs in the forums but never fix them. Prime example is a 4 month old bug that doesn't properly yield rewards. Devs responded to a post about it, yet it remains. Some features simply do not work, and many are very punishing in a way that will actively deprive you of hard earned gains.

-Limited content despite being launched on Epic in 2023. Development for this game is agonizingly slow at a glance. Only 3 levels, very few unique weapons to choose from. 

-Leveling up is unrewarding and bland. You cannot ever improve damage. After 5 hours, all level ups are borderline unnoticable. 

-Stamina system as a whole. Taking damage makes you lose stamina. This means that if you fail to dodge, now you CANNOT dodge. This, on its own, is a baffling choice that is only made worse by half the game's weapons also using stamina when fired. 

-Explanations are borderline nonexistent. This game doesn't hold your hand, and in many ways, that's great. Until you have myriad debuffs that are never once explained, both for yourself and enemies. It is genuinely crazy how little this game tells you about some things while having incessant tips on every loading screen about ONE element type. A basic lorebook would suffice wonderfully for things, as many simply are not clear after even 25 hours and beating all content present. 

-Hit or miss "events". Some are fun and rewarding while others JUST waste your time. Some events are raw, engaging combat, but others are literally following sound cues that don't even always work until you find a tiny item that you have to shoot. It sometimes glitches and hurts you when it shouldn't, then rewards less than 2 dead enemies. 

-Bosses. Seriously, the bosses. I did not stop having fun until I faced my first real boss. My only frustrations with this game have been the bosses. They almost make me want to put my review to a negative. They're terrible. Also vaults. Vault bosses. Just...anything with a boss.

Now, with all those quick cons out of the way-
The good:

-Riveting gameplay loop. I wasn't initially hooked, but once I found a gun I liked, I was enamored. This game truly embodied "Just one more run." Gunplay is tight and snappy in a way that a lot of other titles just miss. Aiming feels buttery smooth and my hits usually go where they should. Killing even the most basic enemies tends to be a satisfying affair that I just want more of. 

-Gorgeous visuals. The world, lighting, effects, and spells look stunning. Except fire. Fire somehow looks pretty lame. But the ice sphere? Beautiful. Running through the world was a delight, especially the more detailed areas. I adore the aesthetic, too. Not seen often. 

-Not too grindy thanks to spell combos that actively increase soul gains. Somewhat counterbalanced by poor leveling system, but still feels nice to cash in your gains often. You get safe, consumable souls that are both valuable and retained after death from enemies and the environment itself. A really nice and rewarding system for exploration. 

-Replayable. The system for upping difficulty (not leveling up your stats) gives reasons to continually revisit past levels and find new things. Very fun to have a reason to go back, even if it's usually not anything too special. 

-Cataclysms. I hated them at first, but they're actually a lot of fun to play with once you understand them. They even give loot to keep the grind going. 

Detail:

This game's difficulty is, for the most part, purely from artificial BS. This game punishes you twice for taking damage. If you get hit, you lose stamina, and not a small chunk. You lose SO much that there's a perk you can get in runs (and JUST for that run) that reduces that by an entire 50% immediately. That's one of the dumbest things I've ever seen in a game. Imagine if you lost stamina in Dark Souls each time you were hit normally. You trade blows with an enemy, then suddenly lack the stamina to dodge. Now you're taking double the damage because you were hit by any number of BS enemy features. Perhaps a teleporting swordsman that LITERALLY came from halfway across the map! Maybe a teleporting sniper? What about a teleporting sniper MINIBOSS? Or perhaps you're in a solid ice dome that stops attacks, but an attack glitched through! Or you're behind a rock that just decided to let an enemy attack through! 

There's a lot of trash that damages you in this game when it shouldn't, or when it's just inconveient. You can learn to play around the teleporting annoyances; that's fine. What you cannot is when the game just doesn't work. Making a build around a Heavy Spell that conjures an impenetrable dome is a ton of fun when it works. But then it just doesn't, and you lose half your health in one attack because this game is a very, very buggy pile of annoyances so very often. You cannot play around the bugs without altering your build, and that is fundamentally terrible.

The bosses are so incredibly easy to describe that it's even more depressing when put into words. They're normal enemies made bigger and given one extra attack. Surprise! Isn't that awesome? Their HP isn't scaled proportionally, though. No, it's about 50x bigger. The entire difficulty of boss fights comes down to their stupidly large HP pools and dumb damage output. That's it. They are exercises in futility and cheese. They are not fun. They are not creative. They are bland. They are absolutely the worst part of this game. They don't even give you many souls. There is GENUINELY no reason to fight them due to how little they yield. It's more time efficient to just never deal with them unless you need them to progress. I made 80k souls in the same mount of time it took me to kill the final boss. It gave me 20k at best, and I don't actually think that's right since I fought 2 cataclysms during it. They blow. They all blow. They are infuriating and boring. There is nothing satisfying about them. 

But the gameplay outside of the bosses? Good GOD does it feel nice. Headshots with lever actions POP small guys and deal fine damage on normal ones. I have a lot of criticisms on the finer details of the weapons, but I don't have the text limit to abide it here. Find a weapon you like, though, and you're in for a good time. I think many weapons need buffs/changes, but all in all, it's still fun. Mixing spells and lead just feels great once you nail your build. Combat flows and you can really get into the flow.

I will say this. The game is fun. I do genuinely like it. I do think it is really cool.

This event comes into play once there are five marks in the top left. 

The way that you can accrue these are:
-Being seen by a specific entity
-Triggering a trap
-Picking up cursed stuff
-Taking damage

For the last one I do not think it is damage specifically it may be 'being hit' or it could have a value system. Being hit by a minion doesn't count as much as being hit by a boss or an elite. I've been hit by attacks that merely launched my character through the air without inflicting any visible damage that have increased the tally. 

What does it do? It creates one of several different events which all cause the sanity bar to deteriorate. In addition a threat will appear; sometimes directly on top of the player character, to make the event more lethal. As far as I have read the event can be defeated, but if you have been taking damage you likely are already in a bad spot to handle an additional higher level challenge than what you have already been facing. 

And that is where the problem I have with it arises. 

If you are having a bad time, this is here to make it worse. It makes it hard for new players to learn the game because if they flub a couple hits they suddenly have to run away from the boss of the level or die and then potentially lose out on progress.

Skilled people can farm it. That's nice, but that doesn't make the event better. It just means that it is effectively 'lose more' mechanic even if that wasn't the design intent. 

Truthfully I have nothing against the event in of itself, but instead with the triggers. If it is meant to be a punishment then it should be better defined and more easy to learn. Failing opt in challenges, intentionally provoking it, or taking too long on the map can all add points to provoke the Calamity. If you want to give it more of a real feel then you can increment it with time, by swiping valuable loot, and by killing important enemies. That way doing more provokes a more aggressive response from the antagonist. Being brazen or risky about it also should serve to further that building animosity. 

It also gives the players something to manage a bit more tangibly as well.

Platted the game today after about 25 hours of time logged (frickin mushrooms <.<) and thought it time to write a review (been awhile since I've done one anyways). With that being said, I'm pretty disappointed with this one as it's a title I've been waiting years for to release here on Steam, but I'll start with the good points of the game (tl;dr at the bottom)

-Gunplay. I think the gunplay is the primary aspect of the game that the devs nailed and is pretty much spot on. Feels quick, fluid, and if done right powerful. Basically like a Destiny shooter but with an inquisition theme as far as actual function is concerned.
-Theme. Artistically, game nails the desired style it was going for. Feels like a Bloodborne-esque game but with an Inquisition fashion rather than a Lovecraftian one.

Unfortunately, this is about where the positives stop. Sorry as it is going to be a bit long winded as there is a fair bit to say about what I personally did not like (again, tl;dr at the bottom).  

-Character development/growth. While the RPG aspects are typical in an almost soulslike design the upgrade system is what I can only describe as gimmicky. Currently the system does [b]NOT[/b] really improve base stats as you go through the upgrade tiers (ie damage value), but rather wholly relies on adding various assortment of novelties that are, in isolation, typically mundane (albeit not always). Which is a major drawback as far as I'm concerned, as this game absolutely loves to spam bullet sponges at you adnauseam. What is required of you, the player, if you wish to succeed is to expand these gimmicks and learn to synergize them into something more useful that is powerful. Sounds like an idea to break the mold right? Here's the problem, you cannot rely on these synergies as there is an RNG aspect to it that is not always going to be at your disposal. It ultimately becomes a "the cards you have been delt" situation. Which will segway to the next point. 

The RNG aspect utilizes Manifestations. Manifestations are more or less a condensed witchfire that drops upon clearing a specified group of mobs which yield a random set of temporary buff/perks to the player (key emphasis on random and temporary). For example, dashing can reload a round into the weapon automatically. However these manifestations have to be re-farmed upon every venture. The RNG of it can be somewhat mitigated by collecting Prophecies that can be equipped to the player's arcanum in order to narrow down the buffs/perks you want into a specified category you may desire for your particular play style. However, it's still random. Didn't get the particular perk you wanted? Tough luck. What would have been a better idea would just have been to allow the manifestations to be permanently affixed to the weapon much like how Destiny did its weapon perks. This would allow for actual builds to be done on the player's end, and give solid and reliable consistency to any given player's play style. I find that kind of system to be far more rewarding and incentivizing as your equipment/weapons now truly have a feeling of weighted value.

-Gameplay. While the gunplay is on point, the gameplay is a whole other story. Gameplay itself is about as shallow as the condensation on your bathroom mirror after a hot shower. Gameplay can be described as following: Spawn mobs > Kill mobs > Collect manifestation > Spawn mobs > Kill mobs > Collect manifestation >Spawn mobs > Kill mobs > Collect manifestation (you get the idea). That's it. That's basically about 90% of the game's entire shtick. The other 10% is mundane treasure hunting used to collect gold, chests to collect things like more treasure for gold, or replenshing items like ammo, etc. The last thing is the event calamities, but guess what that is??? More: Spawn mobs > Kill mobs. Yawn. Even the bosses (save one) are like this. Don't believe me? Go fight the Prophet or the Warrior Priest. Their primary mechanic is... Care to take a wild guess? That's right, spam an army of mobs at you. This is probably my most despised aspect of this game. It is in a phrase, utterly asinine. 

This game is more or less primarily a one trick pony that only knows how to spam mobs at you for the most part, and the spam is to the point it truly feels like this game is meant to be a co-op shooter because that's what it feels like but you're forced to do it solo. I used to solo Destiny raids like Crota for shits and giggles, and that IS what this is going to feel like as it is seemingly desperate to overwhelm you with mobs. It's as if that is almost all it knows how to do. Say what you will, good or bad, but I find this to be completely laughable from a creativity standpoint. 

I'm sure there's a lot of people who find the above appealing and enjoyable in a, for lack of better phrasing, what is more of a loop shooter than an extraction shooter. If that's you, then you'll enjoy this game, but if you're like me and gameplay depth is a must then this is not it. So if you're expecting Destiny Darksouls with an extraction function I think you're going to be sorely disappointed. I know I was. 

tl;dr
Good: Gunplay and art design is awesome. 

Bad: Character development substitutes actual development/growth with gimmicks that relies on interfacing with an RNG mechanic that is essential to clearing the late game. Gameplay is shallow as its idea of gameplay is to only spam hoards of mobs upon you.

...but. it has a ton of flaws and issues that cause a lot of frustration.

> Enemies will spawn directly behind you or next to you. If you're unfortunate enough to have that enemy be an elite, expect instant deaths from out of nowhere.

> Enemies like to teleport around constantly, which wouldn't be so annoying if they couldn't go through walls, instantly reach the top of the map from ground level, or chain teleports away from your character forcing you to chase after them through the map.

> Inconsistent/buggy enemy attack telegraphs. I've had enemies attack me from behind/above with no warning and warnings appear that point in the wrong direction, which can lead to quick deaths.

> Bugged and inconsistent weapons/abilities. I've had spells that don't hit enemies directly in front of me, weapons that straight up don't work some times (Such as the demonic crossbow refusing to bounce between enemies even after multiple shots), or mechanics that are highly inconsistent (Such as stuns from abilities)

> Dots/Item affects that steal kills from your progress. In order to upgrade weapons, you need to get kills in addition to other conditions to level them up, but a lot of the time they work against eachother. For example, there is an item that smites enemies at low health with a lightning bolt. Problem is, that kill doesn't count towards your upgrade progress, so you're gimping yourself by equipping it. Dots such as fire or decay even from the weapon that caused it also won't count towards your kills too, causing a very awkward game of 'don't use your special effects so that you can actually level up'.

> Bugged objectives. There's multiple buried stashes in the game that lead you to treasure, but every single one I've come across was bugged and did not appear after tracking it down. Cursed chests will sometimes spawn enemies out of bounds, and then fail you when you're forced to go out of the range of the chest to get them (Ties in with enemies teleporting away).

> Poor balancing. Certain weapons/upgrades are FAR better than others in comparison, or don't make sense with how they play. Striga has a TON of ammo, does mega damage, is easy to aim, has fast fire rate, and super stagger, but the basilisk (A sniper rifle) has far less range, less damage on headshot, much less ammo, and weak special effects (Slight burn on enemies). Certain arcana have barely any impact on gameplay, such as a measly 10% extra damage on bodyshots.


Overall I love this game and want to see it be improved, but in its current state I'd recommend holding off until full release to see if most of this stuff has been fixed, or picking it up on sale

Hi Witchfire team,

I'm updating my review after spending more time with the Webgrave update, and I wanted to share some thoughts with you. I can tell how much care you've put into this game, and I'm writing this because I genuinely believe Witchfire has the potential to be something special.

Let me start with what I appreciate: the souls-like progression system you're going for makes sense, and I love those games too. The challenge and methodical advancement can be really satisfying when done right. But I think there's a key element missing from how it currently works in Witchfire.

In games like Elden Ring, part of what makes leveling up feel rewarding is that moment when you go back to an area that gave you trouble and just steamroll through it. It's that "wow, look how much stronger I've gotten" feeling that makes all the grinding worthwhile. Right now, your witch defense scaling system prevents that from ever happening. Every time I get stronger, the game immediately adjusts to match me, so I never actually feel more powerful, just differently challenged.

I understand the lore reason - the witch "reorganises her defenses" - but it ends up feeling like the game is working against my progress rather than celebrating it. Especially when the witch supposedly has limited / "very low" influence on the starting island to begin with, the constant scaling feels a bit inconsistent.

The new stats system from the update looks really awesome, but in practice, it still feels like I'm on a treadmill. Leveling costs more and more witchfire while enemies get proportionally tougher, so I'm putting in more effort just to maintain the status quo.

Here's where this really hit me: I decided to try playing a Slayer because the description sounded perfect for my playstyle - "Aggressive Spellcaster" who uses witchcraft in close combat. I was excited to lean into the magic side of the game and really embrace that fantasy.

But then I realised that despite being described as someone who finds "twisted delight in wielding witchcraft", practically nothing has changed. I can barely use spells because witchfire doesn't regenerate naturally. I have to constantly hunt down enemies just to scrape together enough mana to cast anything. I don't even start with a Light spell! I feel like a Gemini witch from The Vampire Diaries - always having to siphon power instead of just using my own. Fun in theory, not so much in practice.

This feels especially odd when you look at the game's own world. The witch uses magic freely, there are clearly powerful magical staffs like Saint Albert's Scepter, and these Preyers are supposedly trained in witchcraft. So why can't a character who's specialised in magic actually use it? How do they even create or power up their magic weapons if they can't use magic themselves without stealing it?

When I compare this to games like Destiny 2 or Remnant 2 that you've presumably drawn inspiration from, those games trust players to use their abilities regularly through natural cooldowns and regeneration. It feels like Witchfire might be a bit too cautious about letting us witchcraft-happy preyers actually feel magical.

What's frustrating about all this is that I can see all the pieces are there for something amazing. The shooting mechanics feel great, the atmosphere is genuinely incredible, and the technical polish is impressive for a team your size. I even noticed you added the DLAA support I had asked for in my Steam review months ago, which shows you're really listening to feedback.

But some of the design choices seem to work against the game's own strengths. Expeditions in the same start areas still feel like survival endurance tests even after I've grown stronger. Good loot drops remain pretty rare. The new rosary beads are a nice addition, though most feel like small percentage bonuses rather than game-changing effects.

One simple idea: what if the Slayer started with a rosary bead that allowed some witchfire regeneration? And instead of a gun like Cricket, we start with something more Witchery like a staff? That alone might solve the magic class experience.

I'm genuinely hoping to be helpful here. Right now it feels like player progression is seen as a problem to solve rather than a reward to give. What if rather than having everything automatically scale up with every "ascension", it instead just means I can choose to tackle bigger challenges? Make the new areas *tough* so we really have to work for it, and just leave the original areas alone so we can come back and feel that power fantasy. If we specialise into a specific character class (like witchery), let us actually feel like a competent magic user. If we read a character description and it promises a certain experience with that class, actually deliver on it so players can feel it as soon as they start.

I really think you have something special here. The core premise is compelling, the world is atmospheric and engaging, and technically it's really solid work. But I think some fundamental adjustments to how progression works - rather than just tweaking numbers - could unlock so much more potential.

I'm still hopeful because I can see what you're building toward, and I want to see it succeed. I just think there's a disconnect between the empowering fantasy the game promises and the constrained reality of how it currently plays. At least from my perspective as someone who wanted to feel the Slayer fantasy but didn't.

I hope this comes across as constructive - you don't need to make things easier, just let progression feel genuinely rewarding and let players feel competent in the roles they've chosen to specialise in.

Thanks for taking the time to read this.

Do not write many reviews but after reading devs most recent patch note response decided I would give it a go. 

Positives: Beautiful environments, variety of weapons, gun play is fun
Negatives: I am going to be speaking specifically about the devs statement about not adding any difficulty settings/sliders. Not going to knock the lack of any coherent plot or story as they did say they were working on that (it is needed,  though lets face it, the action is the king with these kinds of game). Leveling system is simply overly complex as well. 

As a veteran of Dark Souls series, Bloodbourne, Black Myth WuKong and a variety of other challenging games (as all of which I have completed on console) I have found this game quite frustrating and I suspect many others do as well given the comment about refunds the devs made. In each of these above games, progression felt good, your ability to continue to improve to meet and defeat the various challenges thrown your way was frankly way more attainable. Enemy design was fair.I do not need to feel overpowered in a game (though that is kinda fun), just want to be able to find a relatively clear path to get stronger and progress in some reasonable amount of play time (the latter is key). 

The gaming population is trending older (avg age has gone 26 to 36 over the last 20 years) and frankly us old timers (I am 61) have jobs, family, a million other things to do that fill our day. We do not have as much free time and when we do and want to play a game we want one that’s fun, allows for an reasonable challenge, allows for reasonable progression, and has mechanics that are not confusing or take a bunch of reading or YouTubing to figure out. 

This game is simply cumbersome and frankly a bit of a slog.  Leveling takes forever as you get into higher levels, some enemy units are just way overtuned in areas making that progression overly difficult, and you cannot clear an area and then try to get back to an extraction point if you want to escape without going further with your hard earned witch fire without more enemies showing up again (this is in stark contrast to all the games I mentioned above BTW)

The guts for a fun game I think are mostly here, needs more work. A difficulty setting would go a long way to smooth some of these things out and make the game progression much more enjoyable and much more accessible to a bigger consumer base. 

Which brings me to my final point:
I have never understood this mindset of developers who say they will not add difficulty settings/adjust game difficulty. In an industry that seems to be constantly under financial strains, I would think the idea here is to create a good product that is desirable to as many potential customers as possible. It is a business axiom. I get the vision thing and that what you create will not appeal to all gamers (does not need to) but there are rather simple ways to increase your customer base without sacrificing your product and all the hard work and love you have obviously poured into it.

[h1]Identity Crisis[/h1]

The game has a big identity crisis. I'd recommend skipping the Early Access period until the developers balance what's here or decide what type of game they want to make.

Is it a movement shooter like [i]Doom[/i]? Kind of, but no. Not with limited stamina and a useless melee. So why do dozens of enemies spawn out of nowhere?

Is it a Souls-like? Kind of, but no. You're not able to play slowly and deliberately with enemies spawning in behind you. So why do enemies kill you in 3-4 hits?

Is it a monster hunting game? No, but kind of. Bosses will run away/disappear/teleport after taking minimal damage like this is [i]Monster Hunter[/i]. With limited stamina, chasing after retreating bosses just adds tedium. And then more enemies will spawn in behind and around you.

[h1]Difficulty & Combat[/h1]

The "difficulty" in this game this:
- you die in 3 hits
- enemies die in 10-50 hits
- you'll fight 4-15 enemies at a time
- 4-12 enemies will spawn in behind/around you
- at range, your weapons do almost no damage
- at range, enemy weapons still do full damage

I think I ran into about 7 enemy types and killed each hundreds of times. Hopefully, more will be added in the future.

[h1]Progression[/h1]

Gaining levels is very slow, especially after the first few hours. You'll need to dip into and out of the two starting regions numerous times in order to gain enough experience to level up, just so you can take on the more challenging areas. Very repetitive.

Upgrading weapons is very slow. What is a "first mysterium activity" and how do I do it 25 times? I've done it for some weapons without knowing what it is, and 0 times for other weapons. Why not just tell me what this required activity is?

Clearing danger areas is very slow. There's often one enemy that you can't find, that isn't really aggressive, that is the only one left to clear the area. Sometimes, I'm convinced the game is just bugged and the last enemy never spawned in. Very unrewarding.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Not worth $35-$40 USD right now. Maybe when the full game is released. Currently, $20 is probably a fair price for what is offered.

As of the Webgrave update, I can no longer recommend this game. The stat system was significantly nerfed such that, at my same level of 455 prior to the update, I now have 45% less health, 60% less stamina and earn 2.5x less witchfire. You also carry two less healing elixirs for a total of three instead of the previous five. Moreover, each elixir heals you for significantly less while enemies still hit you for the same amount of damage. You can remedy part of this with their new rosary system in which you equip rosary beads, however the stat based ones are weak, you can only equip a few at a time, and they are scattered throughout each map or perhaps earned in other ways.

I feel it is important to continue the discussion around difficulty in gaming and the accessibility challenges it presents. I'm no stranger to difficult games - I've completed Dark Souls, Dark Souls 3, Bloodborne, Sekiro, and Elden Ring to name a few. But I feel these games established a standard of difficulty that can exclude certain players. Witchfire is a difficult and demanding game. But I had found a way round this by leveling up my character, pushing him higher and higher so I could enjoy the game. Even my playstyle changed - I was a long ranged, passive player at early levels, using sniper rifles and freeze spells to slow my enemies. I evolved to blasting my way into enemy camps and taking the challenge head on. But I could do so with the strength I had earned from the levels I earned. 

To make matters worse, the Gnosis difficulty curve system the game incorporates is essential to fully level up to even make it to the end of the game. If I'm struggling at Gnosis level 3 in the current form after the update, then in conjunction with your stat changes I no longer stand a chance on completing the game.

One of the most iconic, if not the most iconic, FPS games is Doom and, too this day, continues to have difficulty levels allowing everyone to access it at a pace that is comfortable to them. The developers of Witchfire have said that they changed their stat system because higher level players were essentially "playing with cheats." I find this statement bizarre. If I'm having fun, what does it matter? The prior stat system allowed everyone to play as they wanted - you could level up as much or as little as you wanted. There was even a video posted by the developers of a very talented player who completed an incredible challenge. Players will always find ways to challenge themselves within the limitations of the game.

I'm more sad and disappointed I have to let this game go. I was following it for years prior to its release. I bought it day one on Epic and bought it again when it came to Steam. I was having so much fun. It breaks my heart to change to a negative review. But this is a warning to casual and even mid-core players who may not enjoy the steep difficulty adjustments with minimal payoff from the new stat system.

[h2]What is an appropriate punishment for taking damage?[/h2]

A well-designed game will comprise a balance of incentives and punishments. You're incentivized to kill enemies through XP drops; you're punished for ignoring enemies when you run yourself into a dead end and have a gaggle of foes on your tail. 

It should go without saying that getting hit is something you want to avoid; you can only do it so many times before it's a game-over, In theory, no further punishment is necessary -- death is its own punishment because it ends your play session and you lose the progress you've been working towards. Surely, then, taking damage should be its own punishment. The Astronauts appear to disagree.

So what happens when you take damage in Witchfire? The first and most immediate effect is that you lose your ability to see [i]sigils[/i], an additional weak point that can be used to immobilize enemies, interrupt attacks, and boost damage. You lose this ability instantly and can only regain it by absorbing witchfire (i.e. killing enemies). You are punished for taking damage by losing access to a powerful ability that could help you turn a bad situation around. [b]The game gets harder temporarily.[/b]

The next thing that happens is that you lose max stamina. Stamina which is used for every action in the game -- shooting, sprinting, jumping, dashing. You now have less leeway. Every action you take must be more considered. You're not able to dodge as often or to shoot for as long. [b]The game gets harder permanently.[/b]

All this pales in comparison to the Calamity mechanic. There's a system in the game, which nobody seems to really understand, where making mistakes (of which "taking damage" seems to be one) will alert The Witch to your presence and she'll cast a curse on you. This curse can take the form of a flying pirate ship that shoots homing balls of energy, or a powerful knight who was actually just an area boss in the previous patch.

Yes, dear reader: taking damage from a boss can trigger the approach of [i]another[/i] boss in addition -- one which will slowly drain your sanity and kill you regardless of your remaining health. [b]The game gets an insane difficulty spike once it already has you on the ropes.[/b]

The developers have explicitly designed the game to work this way. They want you to be at your weakest before the Calamity appears. They think this is fun and that it makes sense in The Lore.

I think I don't care about how much sense it makes.

Witchfire is a strange one. I've been looking forward to it ever since it was announced at the game awards in 2017, but I cannot recommend it in it's current state.

Theprimary game loop is divided into two segments, the hub and expeditions. The hub allows you to level up, research new gear, level up said gear and level up the overall world difficulty and progression by researching Gnosis. This loop feels really solid and you always feel like there's something new to do every time you come back to the hub from an expedition.

The expedition is the second segment. An expedition is basically just choosing which level you want to play and you then set out to collect resources you can use in the hub. Levels are fairly small but open and you choose how you want to tackle each challenge in whichever order you want simply by exploring. Encounters and enemy groups are clearly marked on the map and clearing these will yield resources and temporary buffs. Depending on your Gnosis (world progression) you'll be able to see and interact with more hidden stuff in each level, giving you a reason to come back later as well. Witchfire borrows aspects from extraction shooters as well by robbing you of everything you've collected if you die, so sometimes it's not a bad idea to abort early and try again for the main objective some other time.

Movement is smooth and slick, enemies are varied and well designed and the guns look, sound and feel great. The core loop is phenominal, but Withfire also has some massively negative points towards it.

First off, the environments are simply not designed for combat. You always fight in open fields that sometimes have some debris spread around. Every encounter feels the same and it gets repetetive and boring extremely quickly. Areas feel like they are designed to be traversed through rather than fought in. Despite your flexible movement, there's only ever a single plane of elevation, unless you're fighting on the slope of a hill. Enemies also tend to spawn around you for seemingly no reason. Sometimes you'll be alone only to turn around and notice 10 skeleteons following mere meters behind you. Sometimes they'll spawn when you're already fighting a group of enemies, causing what the game clearly marked as a small encounter to become an overwhelming onslaught. And with the environments being so open, there's oftentimes nowhere to hide as you're suddenly surrounded by 30 riflemen shooting at you from all sides.

The problem is only made worse by the fact that you can only dodge while you have stamina, but taking damage also drains your stamina, leaving you open to the next attack, which then leaves you open to the next attack and so on. Most of the game is actually extremely easy until suddenly it snowballs out of nowhere and you suddenly find yourself completely out of options. Doom 2016 and Eternal reward players with more health the more damage they've taken, allowing players to climb back up from the brink of death and continue fighting, but Witchfire does the complete opposite and it's incredibly frustrating.

Lastly, there's no real narrative to be found beyond the intro cutscene, no story to string me along and keep me interested. This might just be because the game is still in development, but when combat gets repetetive and I feel satisfied with my current gear there's nothing to motivate me through the grind.

I'll be keeping an eye on this game as there are plenty of interesting aspects to it, but as things currently stand I would recommend holding off on it.

Everything in this game requires stamina. Jumping, dashing, sprinting, and even firing many of your guns. However, on taking any damage whatsoever, you lose a sizable chunk of stamina. If you get chipped more than once or twice? You're totally out of stamina, and if you're out of stamina, you can't do much other than walk. It's made infinitely worse by all the things that stop stamina regeneration, like [i]trying[/i] to run, jump, or dash when you haven't yet realized it's all been depleted.

This, in conjunction with oversized hitboxes, insane tracking, and copious status ailments on enemy attacks, strongly encourages an incredibly boring, "safe" playstyle in which you plink away at everything from the longest range possible, as taking even a single hit can rapidly snowball into death.

Basically, if you've played high-level Destiny content, where hand cannons and snipers are king and where you only survive damage phases by standing in an infinite healing pool, then you know exactly what to expect.

Unfortunately, as of the last two updates, the devs seem fully committed to this boneheaded stamina system, so I guess this is a for realsies "Not Recommended" now. It's not that I hate the game, to the contrary I rather like it, but the combination of Souls-like corpse runs with all of this game's various "lose more" mechanics makes playing it a genuinely frustrating experience.

Let me be very blunt: this is an extraction shooter game, but single-player only. If you enjoy games like Helldivers II and Space Marine II, this is a decent game to play as well. However, the lack of multiplayer makes this a very repetitive and boring game, and I find that I can only play one or two runs before quitting out of frustration. I'll explain:

There are many aspects in this game that seem to contradict each other. It's a shooter game, but almost all the enemies don't drop ammunition. You can only obtain ammunition from ammo chests, which are scattered throughout the map, or by killing enemies specifically spawned from the portal. Now, there is also a melee attack, as well as spells you can use to further aid you in killing your enemies, but the main source of damage is your guns. As a result, ammunition is usually the limiting factor from advancing through the map or extracting early.

There are groups of enemies scattered throughout the map. These are alright. However, there seems to be an alert system that spawns more enemies when you kill one in a group, which can quickly get out of hand if you don't expect it. Furthermore, there seems to be no warning. You could kill ten enemies in a row without an alert, but all of a sudden you kill an enemy, and then enemies begin spawning all around you, even if you instakill them. It's annoying, especially because you NEED to kill enemies on the map to progress, so you can't avoid them either. 

The story of this game is very shallow, and it's clear the developers didn't intend on implementing storyline aspects in the game. You are introduced as a 'preyer', who is an agent of a Church. Your goal is to eliminate evil witches and their minions, using guns and spells. That's it. Nothing else. There is no insight into who you are, why you became a preyer, how the world changed around you, etc. Even the Steam description of this game has more story in it: "you play as a wicked inner turned witch hunter on his final mission to reach salvation." But when you get into the game, there is absolutely no mention of this through out the playthrough. You can see hints of the developers' efforts in a half-hearted story by reading the location descriptions and any notes around the maps you get, but the location descriptions are clearly flavor text, and the notes are used to describe the mechanics of the game more than actually providing a story.

In line with the issue of storyline, there is no end-game goal. Let's say you fully clear a map, get all the loot, and extract. Congratulations, you can level up, get new weapons, and go in again. There is no global impact. It doesn't feel rewarding at all. The map just shuffles a bit, and you go again. And again. And again. Eventually, only one clear of a map isn't enough to level up. So, without spending your witchfire (which is used to level up), you must go to another map. And if you die in this map, you drop ALL your loot. Of course, you can pick it up again by going back, but it just feels hopelessly endless without a goal. 

Lastly, there is no multiplayer. I understand that this game is marketed as a single player game, but without storyline, endgame goal, and with more and more enemies that get stronger as you progress, it just feels numbing. What feels worse is that on the developers' FAQ, they specifically stated that they have no plans to implement multiplayer even when fully released. 

Now, a few things to keep in mind: When I wrote this review, I had 11 hours accrued in this game. As I progress, I might find things that would cause my opinion to change. Also, this game is in early access. The developers might read this review and change some things. But until then, this game, in its current state, is, in my opinion, not worth its current price tag of $40.
Game still needs an intense amount of work before i could ever recommend it to anyone.
